name: Maryland Matters
title: What’s so special about the special session? A primer
description: A guide to what's on the table, what's not, what lawmakers need to do, what it all means and what it's going to cost for the planned two-day special session of the General Assembly this week to consider a constitutional amendment on redistricting.
text:
The House of Delegates chamber in regular session in March 2023. (Photo by Bruce DePuyt/Maryland Matters)The General Assembly returns Monday for a special session for the limited purpose of considering a constitutional amendment on how the state draws boundaries for its congressional districts.
A special session is an official gathering of the legislature outside the annual 90-day session that begins each year on the second Wednesday in January. They are not often called, but they’re not all that special either: There have been eight in this century alone, the most recent in December when the House met to elect a new speaker.
The legislature can be called into session by a proclamation of the governor or by a three-fifths vote of the legislature. Gov. Wes Moore issued an executive order calling this session, which was largely a formality after Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) and House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) announced last month that the General Assembly would reconvene Aug. 3 for a special session.
Maryland Matters answers your questions about this latest session.
How long will it last?

	 Special sessions can last up to 30 days, but legislative leaders have been clear that this session is set for Aug. 3-5 and no longer. They are hoping to be done by Tuesday evening, which is National Night Out, an important event for lawmakers to meet and mingle with voters. In a June 16 letter to House members, Peña-Melnyk wrote that she doesn’t expect the session to last more than a couple days.
What can they consider?

	 In theory, anything. In reality, the agenda for this session, as for most special sessions, will be limited to what leadership wants to focus on.
Ferguson and Peña-Melnyk made that clear in a July 20 letter to sent to delegates and senators that said they were directing the Department of Legislative Services “to accept bill drafting requests for the … special session only if they relate to the purpose for which the General Assembly is being reconvened: consideration of legislation concerning redistricting standards.”
Even if a lawmaker was able to take advantage of a special session to push a pet project, the presiding officers can send those bills to committees where they simply will not get a hearing while the other business of the session proceeds.
The chokehold on legislation has upset Republican lawmakers, among others, who had hoped to debate bills focused on pocketbook issues. But with Democrats in firm control of both chambers, and most lawmakers showing little appetite for an extended session, there’s not much the GOP can do about it.
So what will they consider?

	 Lawmakers will consider the proposal for a constitutional amendment to change the way congressional districts are drawn, for one, with identical versions already introduced in the House and the Senate.
But both chambers are expected to consider overrides to a handful of the governor’s vetoes of 2026 legislation. They will also take up legislation that will correct a technical problem of their own making. Both the House and Senate passed bills calling for a constitutional amendment that would make collective bargaining disputes for state workers subject to binding arbitration. Unless one of the bills is withdrawn, it would wind up putting the same question on the November ballot twice, which supporters fear could confuse voters.
What’s the schedule?

	 House and Senate committees that consider elections legislation are scheduled to meet at noon Monday for a joint hearing on the bills in the Joint Hearing Room of the Department of Legislative Services in Annapolis. The House Government, Labor and Elections Committee is expected to hold a voting session immediately after that hearing concludes and the full House could take up the issue later Monday, with Senate action following.
Can I testify?

	 Not unless you signed up to do so on Friday. Legislative leaders required people who wanted to submit testimony or to testify to do so between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on a legislative website Friday. Only 50 people will actually be allowed to testify — in person or virtually — at Monday’s hearing, and they will be limited to two minutes each. If more than 50 signed up to testify, the chairs of the House GLE Committee and the Senate Education, Energy and Environment Committee will choose the 50 speakers.
How many votes will it take?

	 Any proposed constitutional amendment requires approval of three-fifths of the total elected membership of both the 141-member House of Delegates and 47-member Senate. The means it would need 85 votes in the House and 29 in the Senate. With 102 Democrats in the House and 34 in the Senate, passage would seem to be a done deal. But that assumes all lawmakers show up, never a guarantee for a special session called mid-summer, when members may be traveling or on family vacations or tending to their regular jobs. Counting whob actually shows up may be the only tension in the coming session.
What happens if they pass the redistricting bills?

	 Very little, for now. The legislation does not create new congressional districts, and even though the governor and other supporters had been hoping for new congressional district maps to consider, they will not be on the table.
The bills under consideration only deal with the way the state draws its congressional districts. That was thrown into disarray in 2022, when Republicans challenged a redistricting map put forward by Democrats and Judge Lynne Battaglia threw the map out because the districts were not compact and contiguous and respective of natural boundaries. Those standards had previously only been applied to drawing the state’s 47 legislative districts, but not its congressional districts.
The bills would ask voters to approve a constitutional amendment making it clear that the legislative rules do not apply to congressional districts. And making it easier, say, to draw a snaking congressional district or one that leaps from the Eastern Shore across the Chesapeake Bay, which might give Democrats an advantage.
So there won’t be redistricting this fall?

	 Nope. The earliest new congressional district maps could be redrawn is in time for the 2028 elections, and only if lawmakers decide between now and then that it’s worth it. Democrats currently enjoy a 7-1 advantage in the state’s congressional districts, and if the party runs the table in national elections this fall, officials in Maryland may decide it’s not worth the risk or the trouble to redistrict before the next decennial redistricting, for 2032 elections.
Why now?

	 The call for redistricting in Maryland is part of the nationwide tug-of-war between Democratic and Republican states to win seats in a narrowly divided Congress in this fall’s elections. President Donald Trump urged GOP states to redraw district boundaries now — something traditionally done only after the census every 10 years — and Texas answered the call. That sparked a rush among both Democratic and Republican states, with nine states after Texas adopting new congressional maps through legislation, ballot measures and court rulings. Others have been embroiled in legal or political challenges.
The governor appointed a special redistricting commission last fall, and the House passed a redistricting bill in the regular legislative session this spring, but it went nowhere in the Senate. Ferguson bottled the House bill up, saying the risk of a new map outweighed the potential benefits. Any bill would almost surely be challenged in court and could end up with a court-drawn map less favorable to Democrats than the current 7-1 advantage.
That changed this spring when the U.S. Supreme Court handed down its decision in Louisiana v. Callais, which held that racial considerations in congressional redistricting were unconstitutional. Ferguson said the ruling “gutted the Voting Rights Act,” and that “the rules had changed” in light of the court’s ruling.
What’s all this going to cost?
There’s no free lunch, as the saying goes, and the same goes for the special session. Exact costs won’t be known until after, but a  back-of-the-envelope estimate, based on legislative analysis of special sessions in 2012, 2019 and 2021, would put the cost around $39,528.

It’s not nothing, but in Maryland’s $27.7 billion budget it amounts to about to 14 cents of every $100,000 spent.


The 47 senators and 141 delegates aren’t paid but are entitled to the normal reimbursements and perks they receive during the regular session. Those include hotel rooms for some, mileage for those who live too close to get the hotel room benefit, and a meal per diem. Legislators are not required to submit receipts.


The meal per diem is $63 per day. If all lawmakers take it for two days of a special session, that’s about $23,688. But it appears not all lawmakers take the full reimbursement, based on past accounting. In 2021, for example, the General Assembly paid out $22,507 for lawmakers’ meals over a five-day session, or $4,501 per day. Based on that average, add $9,003 for the coming two days.


Hotel reimbursements are capped at about $125 per day. The legislature is authorizing one night initially though a small number of lawmakers might get two if they have to come in on Sunday night. Receipts are required.


Based on past usage, about 75% of 188-member legislature could take the hotel reimbursement: In 2018, about 76% of all members got a room, and about 74% did so for the special session of 2021. If 75%, or 141 lawmakers, get a room for one night this week, the bill comes to about $17,625. That number increases if the session requires another overnight stay.



In 2021, the General Assembly paid out $8,689 for mileage and parking for the special session to 49 lawmakers or an average of $183.15 per lawmaker over five days. Based on that average, the 47 lawmakers who didn’t take a hotel room in the earlier estimate would get $35.47 a day in this session. For two days, that would total $3,443. That number is not adjusted for inflation and the breakdown of mileage and parking is not incuded in a Department of Legislative Services analysis.



There are other costs, such as the potential cost of staff overtime. In 2021, special session overtime costs for staff ran about $1,738 per day over the five days. Adjusted for inflation, that same amount would work out to more than $2,081 per day. Factor in a minimum of one day.


A new factor is the cost of livestreaming the session. Those video and audio broadcasts are handled by Maryland Public Television. In 2021, it cost $3,080 per day. Adjusted for inflation, the cost would run about $7,378.52 for two days.


That makes the average cost per day for a two-day special session about $19,764.

name: WyoFile
title: The Trump administration is ranching the taxpayers
description:
It’s asinine to put cattle back into retired allotments with grizzlies, which will lead to livestock losses compensated by the public, writes guest columnist Kelsey Yarzab Yates.
The post The Trump administration is ranching the taxpayers appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
It’s pretty clear from the latest move to put cattle back onto retired grazing allotments that ranchers are intent on farming the taxpayer. It will come at the expense of our public lands, wildlife habitat and the native species that live there. 

Opinion

And it’s not like anyone was forced off the 31,000 acre grazing allotment in the Upper Green River Valley known as the Elk Ridge complex, roughly 30 miles southeast of Jackson. That land was retired from grazing in a buyout with sheep producers in 2016. The buyout aimed to alleviate issues with domestic sheep grazing, which poses a threat to native bighorn sheep through disease spread and competition for grass. 
Now the U.S. Forest Service is ready to open up the land to cattle producers. The Trump administration claims that will compensate producers for grass lost to last year’s Dollar Lake Fire. 
But the blaze occurred a year ago. Didn’t that give area ranchers time to plan, adjust their herd size accordingly or look for private grass? Why would they want to put cattle into an area with a history of depredations by grizzly bears? 
The answer is simple: In Wyoming, we’ve created an incentive program for ranchers to lose livestock to native carnivore species. Our livestock loss program pays a “multiplier” of up to three and a half times the market value of a stock animal. And we spend a lot of money on range riders who spend the bulk of their time riding the range and looking for lost animals to get the publicly funded compensation dollars. 
A basic fact of being in business is that you suffer losses. Walmart suffers significant shoplifting loss, and yet we don’t see the government compensating the company for it — and certainly not paying triple the value. Any executive would jump at the chance to drive up profits like that, and work to demonstrate the losses to collect the check. 
I understand that there are livestock loss programs across the globe, and there are strong arguments to maintain them. However, the allotments in the Upper Green River were retired from livestock grazing to solve recurring problems — the contact between native bighorn sheep and domestic sheep that can lead to disease spread, as well as loss of livestock to grizzly bears — and willing parties agreed. Now we’re working to go right back to creating a problem, costing us public money. 
We hear all the time that grizzly bears can’t be allowed everywhere — like in the middle of towns. Fair enough. But at the same time, we shouldn’t have cattle and sheep everywhere, especially on lands where losses are inevitable, and taxpayers will foot the bill.
A grizzly bear forages near Togwotee Pass on May 19, 2020, in Teton County. (Ryan Dorgan)
We know how this will play out. Cattle are going to die. Then bears will die. And finally, taxpayers are going to foot the bill for a policy that puts the interests of a small group of public land grazers over the broader interests of everyone, the land itself and wildlife. 
This is the vision the Trump administration has for millions of acres of public lands throughout the West — cattle and sheep everywhere. They’ve said they want to put 500,000 more animal units on public lands. That will include wildlife rich areas in which grazing was ended for legitimate reasons. 
As a Wyoming resident, taxpayer and lover of our public lands and wildlife, this policy represents a massive giveaway to a small group of people at the expense of the vast majority of Americans who own and cherish these public resources.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: New nuclear campus deal would require Idaho to accept, store spent nuclear fuel, radioactive waste
description: Idaho would be required to accept spent nuclear fuel and high-level radioactive waste if the state becomes one of the U.S. Department of Energy’s new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses.  On Tuesday, Department of Energy officials announced that Idaho was one of five states selected as a potential host-site for a new nuclear campus, joining Utah, […]
text:
A 2023 aerial shot of the Materials and Fuel Complex at the Idaho National Laboratory's desert site. The complex contains several specialized labs where INL researches nuclear fuels. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho National Laboratory)Idaho would be required to accept spent nuclear fuel and high-level radioactive waste if the state becomes one of the U.S. Department of Energy’s new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses. 
Idaho selected as potential host site for new DOE Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus 

On Tuesday, Department of Energy officials announced that Idaho was one of five states selected as a potential host-site for a new nuclear campus, joining Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma and Louisiana. 
Federal officials said the nuclear campuses will boost manufacturing, create jobs, promote American energy independence and attract financial investment. 
But to move forward, the state of Idaho would need to enter into a host agreement with the federal government to accept spent nuclear fuel and waste from other states. 
“The host agreement shall provide for the acceptance of out-of-state used nuclear fuel,
spent nuclear fuel, and high-level radioactive waste,” states a memorandum of understanding between the U.S. Department of Energy and the state of Idaho that Gov. Brad Little signed July 24. 
On Wednesday, the Idaho Statesman reported that the three states selected for the nuclear campuses would each take one-third of the United States’ stockpile of spent nuclear fuel.
 Idaho’s 1995 ‘Batt Agreement’ called for limiting spent nuclear fuel from coming into the state

Thirty years ago, the state of Idaho reached a 1995 settlement agreement with the federal government that was signed by the late former Gov. Phil Batt that was aimed at preventing Idaho from becoming a permanent dumping ground for the nation’s nuclear waste. The so-called Batt Agreement called for limiting shipments of spent nuclear fuel into Idaho and expediting the treatment and permanent removal of spent nuclear fuel and nuclear waste from Idaho, according to an explanation posted to the U.S. Department of Energy’s website. 
The memorandum of understanding that Little signed July 24 requires Idaho and the U.S. Department of Energy to “address any issues related to the 1995 Idaho Settlement Agreement and related addenda and supplemental agreements, in a mutually agreeable manner, prior to the effectiveness of the Host Agreement.”
Idaho Lt. Gov. Scott said the state has modified the settlement agreement several times over the past 30 years, including a waiver in 2025 to allow research on shipments of spent nuclear fuel sent to Idaho. 
Modifying the agreement again to align with the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovations Campus agreements wouldn’t be a problem, Bedke said. 
“If we are going to continue to be a leader in the nuclear space, and our speciality (at Idaho National Laboratory) is recycling nuclear fuel, then it makes sense you are going to bring in other used fuel to recycle,” Bedke said Friday. 
Idaho Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke, R-Oakley, recites the Pledge of Allegiance on the Senate floor on Jan. 7, 2025, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“Naturally the agreement has got to be modified to acknowledge what the world looks like in 2026, particularly with Idaho National Laboratory being one of the leaders in nuclear testing and innovation,” Bedke said. 
Bedke said he supports taking the next step with the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus selection process. 
“This is a good opportunity for Idaho, but none of this will shortcut the safety of Idaho’s environment, including our aquifer,” Bedke said. “We’re not going to be putting the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer at risk.”
Over the 30 years since the 1995 settlement agreement, Bedke said many perspectives on nuclear energy have changed. 
“This is not waste,” Bedke said. “We throw that term around, but this is fuel that can be recycled and used for good purposes.” 
Efforts to reach the Idaho Attorney General’s Office and Idaho Gov. Brad Little’s office for comment were unsuccessful. Little did issue multiple statements supporting the partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy and the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses.
 Idaho’s ‘nuclear watchdog’ says deal is all about finding a place to store nuclear waste

Leigh Ford, executive director of the Snake River Alliance, said she is concerned the new nuclear campuses are driven by a desire to get states to agree to accept and store nuclear waste as President Donald Trump pushes for a nuclear energy renaissance.

Idaho is honored to be one of five contenders for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus. Thank you to President @realDonaldTrump, @SecretaryWright, and @ENERGY for recognizing Idaho’s leadership in nuclear innovation.
Together, we’ll power America’s energy future. https://t.co/povZiyLOKE
— Brad Little (@GovernorLittle) July 28, 2026

“I think this is the fifth iteration of the Department of Energy trying to deal with nuclear waste,” Ford said Friday.
“They have to indicate they know what to do with the radioactive waste,” she added. 
The Snake River Alliance is a Boise-based nonprofit organization that describes itself as “Idaho’s nuclear watchdog and clean energy champion.”
“It’s very concerning, not only for the transportation risk, but Idaho already has a huge radioactive burden,” Ford said. “We are a downwind state. I’ve been traveling the state getting people signed up for the Radioactive Exposure Compensation Act. It’s been devastating to see all families be affected (by exposure to radiation downwind from nuclear test sites). There will be more of a burden if this happens.”
Ford said Idahoans should voice opposition to the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses to their local elected officials and ask questions about protecting water and land.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Real estate conference to recognize $158M Omaha library project, five ‘hall of fame’ pros
description: Nebraska’s largest annual conference of real estate and development experts, now in its 37th year, is poised to recognize Omaha’s new $158 million public library as its pick for a project with extraordinary rippling impact.
text:
The Omaha Central Library at 72nd and Dodge Streets is the 2026 CRE Summit choice for its "Summit Award" winner. The Commercial Real Estate Summit is to be held Aug. 21 at the downtown CHI Health Center, and organizers expect roughly 900 participants. The lifted corners on east and west sides of the new library were designed to mimic the opening of a book. (Photo courtesy of APMA, HDR, Tom Harris)OMAHA — Nebraska’s largest annual conference of real estate and development experts, now in its 37th year, is poised to recognize Omaha’s new $158 million public library as its pick for a project with extraordinary rippling impact.
Inside the Central Library (Photo courtesy of APMA, HDR, Tom Harris)
Omaha Central Library, which saw roughly 145,000 visitors in its first two months after opening in April, is to receive the top “Summit Award” at the CRE Summit to be held Aug. 21 at CHI Health Center in downtown Omaha. 
The 102,000-square-foot structure is said to be one of the largest philanthropic investments in a public library system in recent history — built with private dollars plus $20 million from the City of Omaha. The city is to cover costs of ongoing operations.
Architecturally distinct and with a “book robot” officials said is the first of its kind for a U.S. library, the project hit a “home run” in meeting criteria that includes size, innovation, economic growth and regional impact, said Chris Mensinger, summit co-chair. She said the new library serves as a “connector” for residents of the state’s largest city.
“With the location at 72nd and Dodge it’s accessible citywide and provides top-of-the-line technology, access to information and art to inspire us to learn and connect with one another,” Mensinger said.
A library team including designers and the nonprofit fundraiser is to be recognized, along with four new inductees to the CRE Summit “Hall of Fame,” during the summit event expected to draw some 900 Omaha and Lincoln area business, policy-makers and real estate leaders to hear experts and discuss trends of the commercial real estate market. 
Asked what’s different this year, Mensinger said organizers plan a greater push to elicit solutions from “people in the room.” Topics at the all-day event include business recruitment, AI challenges and affordable housing.
Omaha’s 2025 CRE Summit is expected to draw up to 900 commercial real estate professionals and fans. Shown here is a previous event. (Courtesy of Omaha CRE Summit)
Another key workshop topic is Nebraska tools and laws aimed at bolstering economic development, including “Community Improvement Districts.” Recently approved by the Nebraska Legislature, CIDs are zones inside a city’s boundaries where property owners essentially tax themselves to fund infrastructure and public improvements.
The town of Blair just broke ground on the state’s first CID effort, a 137-unit Bear Creek residential project. Developers believe the price of a house there could drop by as much as 30% by applying the new provisions. 
Headline speaker is Spencer Levy, a Baltimore-based senior economic advisor for CBRE, who summit leaders describe as a nationally recognized industry voice with the most downloaded podcast on commercial real estate globally.
 

Among Central Library highlights:

In its first two months, library officials said more than 80,000 items were borrowed and about 7,600 new library cards issued.


An arm of a robotic machine stretches multiple stories to retrieve books and other library materials from more than 4,000 metal bins stacked in a storage vault. The so-called “automated storage and retrieval system” stores up to 600,000 items and was reported to be a first among public U.S. libraries. 
On site are about 300 parking spaces, 16 meeting rooms, an outdoor garden, a floor for genealogy and local history, a podcasting room, a children’s area, a drive-thru window for library material pickups and drop offs.
Materials  from the Do Space, a technology library that stood at the site since 2013 until it was demolished to make way for the new facility, have been integrated into the Central Library.




Levy chairs the research committee for the Real Estate Roundtable, a public policy advocate for the U.S. commercial real estate industry. That position often  puts him in front of national elected officials and policy makers.
Jerry Slusky, summit founder and co-chair, said Levy is expected to address challenges including housing demand, changing interest rates, high construction costs and office market disruption related in part to remote work.
Slusky started the conference in 1990 when, while teaching a real estate course at Omaha’s Creighton University, he lamented to the dean about the lack of awareness about the Resolution Trust Corp. created to help fix the 1980s financial crisis. The dean challenged him to put together a workshop, which evolved into today’s more wide-ranging summit that draws business leaders as well.
The Summit Award last year went to the Catalyst project, a 170,000-square-foot co-working hub for health care and technology businesses in midtown Omaha. Organizers presented the inaugural Summit Award in 2017 to the University of Nebraska Medical Center and Nebraska Medicine. Other winners included Tri-Faith Initiative, NuStyle Development and Kiewit Corp.
This year’s winner rose at the former site of Do Space, one of the nation’s first technology libraries that opened at the southwest corner of 72nd and Dodge Streets in 2015 and was demolished to make way for the Central Library. Do Space technologies and materials were incorporated into the new facility.
As Central Library was planned, controversy swirled around what then was Omaha’s main public library downtown, the W. Dale Clark Library. That structure was demolished to make way for the $600 million Mutual of Omaha skyscraper just west of the Gene Leahy Mall at the Riverfront. A streetcar running from downtown to midtown was key to Mutual’s decision, supported by then Mayor Jean Stothert, to build the tower on the property.
A smaller downtown library branch eventually opened in a renovated structure farther south, nearer to the Old Market at 14th and Jones Streets. 
Just across Dodge street to the north, a separate Crossroads mixed-use campus is slowly underway, including a more recently announced element, Omaha’s proposed joint police and fire administrative headquarters.
Central Library was designed by HDR and Alley Poyner Machhietto Architecture. Other project partners included nonprofits Heritage Omaha, the primary fundraiser, the Omaha Public Library Foundation and Do Space. The library is part of the Omaha public library system.
 



2026 Hall of Fame
Deb Graeve-Morrison (Courtesy of CRE Summit)
Also to be featured during the summit are the four 2026 CRE Summit “Hall of Fame” inductees who summit representatives say have led influential deals and helped transform communities. They are: Deb Graeve-Morrison, former president of NAI NP Dodge; Doug Nodgaard of Equitable Bank of Nebraska; Ember Grummons, investment sales broker at Investors Realty; and Michael Moylan, founder and president of Shamrock Development. 
Graeve-Morrison’s experience dates to 1991. Prior to joining NAI NP Dodge in 2010, she was executive vice president of commercial real estate at Seldin Company. Summit representatives said she is known for managing high-profile, multi-market real estate projects and
Doug Nodgaard (Courtesy of CRE Summit)
advocating for women and young professionals to create a more inclusive industry. 
Nodgaard, Omaha market president of Equitable Bank, worked on projects including Omaha’s first major downtown condo development that helped reintroduce residential living to the city’s urban core, said summit organizers. They said his relationship-focused approach to commercial lending helped provide capital for development that has contributed to the area’s expansion.
Ember Grummons (Courtesy of CRE Summit)
Grummons, in the industry since 1993, specializes in the sale and acquisition of investment property including office buildings, shopping centers, multi-tenant industrial properties throughout the Midwest. Summit officials say he has closed hundreds of millions of property, leading transactions including the sale of metro area properties such as North Park office buildings and Oakview Plaza and Metro Crossing shopping centers.
Moylan and partners developed or acquired more
Mike Moylan (Courtesy of CRE Summit)
than 1.7 million square feet of Omaha mixed-use, retail, office and industrial properties, with a primary focus on downtown. He was lead developer of the $205 million-plus Capitol District. Other notable projects include 1000 Dodge, Paxton Condominiums, Keeline Building and the recently acquired Old Mill Centre.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Top officials leave hospital rate-setting commission amid AHEAD model transition
description: As Maryland begins the transition into a new hospital rate-setting system, the state commission authorized to establish those rates is heading into its own transition – a change in leadership.
text:
Gov. Wes Moore appointed former Maryland Health Secretary Joshua Sharfstein to lead the Health Services Cost Review Commission in 2023. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)As Maryland begins the transition into a new hospital rate-setting system, the state commission authorized to establish those rates is heading into its own transition – a change in leadership.
Health Services Cost Review Commission Chair Joshua Sharfstein and executive director Jon Kromm said the the July 22 meeting of the HSCRC would be their last with the commission.
Their departure marks a significant leadership change at the powerful state body that determines how much hospitals can charge for care. Both have been with the commission since 2023.
During those years, Sharfstein, Kromm and HSCRC staff negotiated with federal officials under the Biden and Trump administrations about the future of Maryland’s hospital rate-setting model. The previous model, called the Total Cost of Care, expired at the end of 2025, leading into the Achieving Healthcare Efficiency through Accountable Design system, also called the AHEAD model.
“I feel that this model provides an opportunity to better health and lower costs for Maryland,” Sharfstein said in a recent interview.
Sharfstein, a former Maryland Health secretary, is currently a vice dean at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. He was initially expected to step away in June but stayed on for one more month, which coincided with Kromm’s last meeting as well.
Kromm will be returning to Health Management Associates, a research and consulting firm focusing on the healthcare industry, where he was a managing principal prior to joining the commission in 2023. William Henderson, principal deputy director with the commission, will take over as interim executive director. A new chair has not been announced.
But Kromm and Sharfstein’s departure means the HSCRC will be under new leadership during the multiyear shift into the AHEAD model after years of negotiations with two presidential administration to nail down the new framework.
The state’s previous hospital rate-setting system technically came to an end Dec. 31 — though major changes in state operation have not yet occurred. The Total Cost of Care system gave Maryland officials authority to regulate hospital costs across all payers in the system, which include private insurance, Medicaid and Medicare. The Health Service Cost Review Commission determines those rates.
Kromm (far left) joined Gov. Wes Moore and CMS Administrator Chiquita Brooks-LaSure at the signing of the first agreement for the federal AHEAD model on Nov. 1, 2024. The Trump administration decided to rework that agreement months later. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
State and federal officials had signed an agreement in 2024 that would have largely kept the state’s authority to regulate all payers intact. But the Trump administration decided early last year to renegotiate the terms of that agreement.
State and federal officials went back and forth over how much authority Maryland should have to dictate hospital rates, and federal officials looked to remove Maryland’s ability to set the rates for care provided under Medicare, an authority the state had held for more than 40 years.
Ultimately, the state was allowed to keep much of its hospital payment system for two years, allowing time to implement larger policy changes before revoking the state’s authority to set Medicare rates in 2028.
The challenge for HSCRC’s future leadership will be in how to implement AHEAD model goals, such as keeping the costs of healthcare low and strengthening Maryland’s primary care system.
But if there’s going to be a leadership change at the HSCRC, now is the time, said Gene Ransom, CEO for MedChi, the Maryland State Medical Society.
“It kind of makes sense,” he said. “Now, it’s time to move into implementation. It’s logical that you would have a turnover at this time.
“You have high-level staff who are staying on and are really talented. I think everything should be fine,” he said. “It’s a natural course of things.”
Sharfstein’s departure also closes the chapter on his controversial appointment to the commission.
In June 2023, Gov. Wes Moore announced the appointment of three commissioners to the HSCRC, which included Sharfstein and Nicki McCann, vice president of provider/payer transformation for the Johns Hopkins Health System.
Sharfstein’s appointment was in question due to a Maryland law that says there cannot be more than three commissioners with connections to “the management or policy of any facility” on the HSCRC to avoid potential conflicts of interest. Additionally, a 1995 ethics decision concluded that a commission employee’s affiliation with Johns Hopkins University violated a state employment conflict law, given the close relationship between the university and Johns Hopkins Health System.
With two other hospital representatives already on the commission, the question was whether Sharfstein and McCann’s appointments violated that three-person limit.
The Moore administration stood by the appointments, saying that Sharfstein and McCann met “all the statutory requirements to serve on the Commission.” Months later, Moore appointed Sharfstein to serve as chair.
Moore appointees to Md. hospital cost review commission in doubt due to legal questions

Sharfstein’s appointment also coincided with criticisms over the commission’s gender parity, with only one woman filling a seat on the seven-member board at the time. Today, there are two women serving on the commission.
Meanwhile, members of the insurance industry voiced concern that there were transparency issues in some of the decision-making at the HSCRC with Sharfstein as chair, during AHEAD negotiations and other policy decisions.
This past session, the governor’s office did not ask the Maryland Senate to reappoint Sharfstein to the commission, leaving his tenure with the HSCRC to expire this summer.
At the July meeting, Kromm applauded the work of the HSCRC under Sharfstein’s leadership.
“He and I have worked together in a number of contexts, on a number of really tricky policy issues. I am really fortunate to call him a friend,” Kromm said at the July meeting. “I’ve learned an incredible amount from Josh over the years. I will forever be indebted to you for all that you’ve provided both to me personally, to the staff here through your leadership and all the great work you’ve done.”
In his final remarks, Kromm thanked the work of the commission staff, a small group that he said “doesn’t get a lot of flowers” for working on the challenging policy that comes out of the HSCRC.
He also thanked the remaining commissioners who “have a tremendously hard voluntary job,” and noted that the commission have “challenges ahead” as the state transitions to the model.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: After contract dispute with East Idaho hospital, Legislature’s task force to study health insurers
description: After a major health insurer dropped an East Idaho hospital from its network, Idaho Republican legislative leaders founded a new working group of state lawmakers tasked with studying the practices of health insurance companies. The formation of the taskforce, formally called the Idaho Health Insurers Working Group, came partly in response to lawmakers’ conce[...]
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)After a major health insurer dropped an East Idaho hospital from its network, Idaho Republican legislative leaders founded a new working group of state lawmakers tasked with studying the practices of health insurance companies.
The formation of the taskforce, formally called the Idaho Health Insurers Working Group, came partly in response to lawmakers’ concerns over the contract dispute fallout, said House Speaker Mike Moyle, one of the highest-ranking Republican lawmakers. Half of the eight-member task force are from East Idaho. 
Rep. Soñia Galaviz, D-Boise, makes a comment during the House Education Committee meeting on Jan. 14, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. Also pictured is Rep. Chris Mathias, D-Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
But it’s also in response to statewide concerns, said Rep. Soñia Galaviz, the sole Democrat appointed to the task force. 
“I too am hearing concerns about health insurance and being denied claims or particular bureaucratic struggles, just a lot of hoops to jump through when you’re trying to get prior authorization or a claim approved, or particular tensions with any given provider or hospital,” the Boise Democrat said. “And so the concerns go beyond Eastern Idaho.”
In an interview on Friday, Moyle said that he and Senate President Pro Tempore Kelly Anthon founded the task force a couple weeks ago. Its first meeting is slated for Aug. 11, with no time or agenda set yet. 
In the weeks leading up to the shakeup in East Idaho health care coverage, the insurer, Regence, argued the for-profit owners of the hospital, Portneuf Regional Medical Center, was asking for an unreasonable pay increase. But the hospital said Regence denied the vast majority of its claims, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Regence runs Idaho’s state employee health insurance plan, covering more than 20,000 state employees and their family members. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 What will the task force focus on?

The website for the new task force lays out an ambitious mission, saying it is charged with studying “the performance of health insurers in Idaho, but not limited to their rates of claim denial and yield on expected reimbursement to providers, delays in treatment caused by prior authorization decisions and related practices, and the amount insurers owe to providers in accepted but unpaid claims,” along with studying “the effect of poor health insurer performance on the health of Idahoans” and making recommendations to the Legislature “on policy solutions to poor health insurer performance.”
Idaho House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star, answers a reporter’s question during a press conference on Jan. 6, 2025, at the Statehouse in Boise. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
But Moyle outlined an even bolder vision: A broad look at addressing health care affordability, including an understanding of how different actors, including medical providers, contribute to costly care for patients. 
“What I’ve learned in politics: A lot of time we jump to conclusions. We think it’s one thing, and then we do our homework and find out, ‘Oh my goodness, we were wrong. It was something different.’ And that I think may be the case with this,” Moyle said in an interview. 
Two lawmakers from East Idaho are set to co-chair the committee: Rep. Dustin Manwaring from Pocatello, and Sen. Mark Harris from Soda Springs. The committee includes two other East Idaho lawmakers: Sen. Kevin Cook from Idaho Falls, and Rep. Josh Wheeler from Ammon.
The remainder of the committee is from North Idaho — Sen. Carl Bjerke from Coeur d’Alene, and Rep. Cornel Rasor from Sagle — or from southwestern Idaho — Galaviz and Sen. Josh Keyser from Meridian.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Blackburn moves $4.8M from US Senate campaign account in apparent legal ‘workaround’
description: A political action committee operated by officers of the conservative pro-private school voucher group Club For Growth has spent $4.81 million backing U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s gubernatorial bid, months after Blackburn donated a nearly identical amount to the organization’s primary PAC, campaign finance reports show. In May, Blackburn nearly emptied her f[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, pictured above, nearly depleted her campaign account when she donated $4.8 million to the Club for Growth Action PAC in May. (Photo: John Partipilo)A political action committee operated by officers of the conservative pro-private school voucher group Club For Growth has spent $4.81 million backing U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s gubernatorial bid, months after Blackburn donated a nearly identical amount to the organization’s primary PAC, campaign finance reports show.
In May, Blackburn nearly emptied her federal campaign account, donating $4.8 million to the Club for Growth PAC.
Tennessee Freedom Fund, one of several PACs with close ties to Club for Growth, has been purchasing TV advertisements praising Blackburn and attacking her opponent, U.S. Rep. John Rose, since June.
Under Tennessee law, Blackburn is not allowed to directly spend her U.S. Senate campaign money in the governor’s race. Federal law does not prohibit the transaction.
“It clearly reads as a workaround to get her remaining federal campaign war funds into the state race,” said Brendan Glavin, the director of insights with OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan organization that tracks political spending.
Club for Growth operates multiple federal and state PACs that are referred to as independent expenditure groups. These groups are allowed to raise and spend unlimited funds supporting or opposing candidates, as long as they don’t coordinate with the campaigns they’re helping.

 How the money flows
The group purchasing advertisements to support Blackburn is called the Tennessee Freedom Fund PAC, and formed on Feb. 10, 2026, according to state campaign finance records.
The School Freedom Fund transferred a total of $4.81 million to the Tennessee Freedom Fund, a state-based political action committee, in June and July 2026.
Blackburn’s Senate campaign made a $4.8 million donation to the Club for Growth Action PAC on May 8, 2026, according to FEC records.
The Tennessee Freedom Fund, School Freedom Fund and Club for Growth Action, which support candidates who advocate for private school vouchers, all list the same treasurer and are registered to the same Washington, D.C., address. The address is also the office address of Club for Growth.
Billionaire Jeff Yass is the primary funder of Club for Growth and the School Freedom Fund and has been a donor to Blackburn since her first campaign for Congress in 2002. 

The Tennessee Freedom Fund PAC and Club for Growth Action PAC are both registered to the same Washington, D.C., address and have the same listed officers, Club for Growth CEO David McIntosh and CFO Adam Rozansky, according to federal and state campaign records.
Glavin said the layering of money makes it seem like the cash supporting Blackburn is “technically coming from another source.”
“But it is hard to ignore the obvious connection between the transactions,” Glavin said.
The Lookout asked Blackburn’s campaign manager, Abigail Sigler, specific questions about the donation and the various transactions. Sigler did not answer any of the questions.
The Lookout made multiple attempts to reach Club for Growth, including sending detailed questions about transactions and whether the donations were connected. A Club for Growth staff member answered the Lookout’s phone call Friday and said they would “get back” to us with a response. As of publication, no one from Club for Growth has answered our questions.
A dismissed complaint
Blackburn began telling people close to her she planned to run for governor in December 2024, but she didn’t make an official announcement until August 2025.
Following her November 2024 Senate reelection, Federal Election Commission records show, she continued to fundraise and spent $3.2 million in Senate campaign funds in 2025. Her spending pace was similar to what she spent during the 2024 Senate election, even though her next reelection bid wouldn’t come until 2030.
Gary Loe, a longtime Knoxville Republican activist, filed a complaint earlier this year with the state campaign finance regulator accusing Blackburn of using her Senate account to pay for advertisements, staff and travel that would help her run for governor before she announced her candidacy.
The state campaign finance board dismissed Loe’s complaint, finding that Blackburn is allowed to operate both accounts, and that because she wasn’t officially a gubernatorial candidate, they couldn’t weigh in on her Senate spending. The board declared any complaints over her federal spending would have to be made to the FEC. No FEC complaint has been filed.
State funds in federal races
Over the past decade, former state Sen. Brian Kelsey and former state House Speaker Beth Harwell both faced ethics complaints related to how they moved state campaign funds to groups helping them in federal races.
Kelsey, during his 2016 failed bid for a U.S. House seat, moved around $106,000 from his state campaign account through several PACs, eventually reaching the American Conservative Union, which purchased radio advertisements to boost his election.
Prosecutors detailed the lengths to which Kelsey went to conceal the money’s movements as a reason for bringing the case forward.
Kelsey pleaded guilty to two counts of campaign finance violations. He served two weeks in prison before President Donald Trump pardoned him.
Harwell agreed to pay a $16,000 fine after she moved $47,000 from two state campaign PACs to a federal super PAC that bought ads attacking one of her primary opponents in a failed 2022 bid for U.S. Congress.
Both these transactions were moves from state accounts to benefit federal races, which the FEC explicitly bans.
Sam Stockard contributed to this report.
