name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Towns surrounding the Quabbin Reservoir protect the water for 2.7 million people in Eastern Mass. They’re getting financially starved in the process.
description: The state’s payments in lieu of taxes system treats Quabbin land as nearly worthless. In reality, it's the most valuable land in Massachusetts: Without it, more than 2.7 million people across Eastern Massachusetts -- 40 percent of the state's population -- would have no water.
text:
For nearly a century, residents in the towns around the Quabbin Reservoir have faithfully upheld one of our Commonwealth’s most profound collective commitments: safeguarding clean, reliable water for Eastern Massachusetts. Although residents of those towns are, ironically, not given access to the water they protect and provide to some 2.7 million fellow Massachusetts residents, they have done this responsibly and at tremendous cost. Now, that cost has become unsustainable. 
Take the town of Shutesbury, a Massachusetts community of 1,800 people on the western shore of Quabbin. One of every three acres in the town is held by the Commonwealth to protect the reservoir. That land is permanently blocked from development, permanently removed from the town’s tax base—and permanently vital to the survival of Boston and the other Eastern Massachusetts communities the reservoir serves. Yet the financial arrangement that compensates Shutesbury for this sacrifice treats the land as almost worthless, and costs Shutesbury residents over $3 million every year. 
Shutesbury’s fiscal year 2026 town budget was $7.8 million. Like many towns, it depends on ever-increasing residential property taxes to pay that cost. Unlike many towns, it cannot slow those tax increases through development.  
Shutesbury lacks a commercial or industrial tax base and the capacity to build substantial amounts of new housing because it has no public water supply (even with Quabbin literally in the town) and because most land suitable for such development is within the one-third of town taken by the Commonwealth for the reservoir. The result for all the Quabbin towns is a budget crisis that has become an existential threat, with schools facing closure, roads and bridges left unrepaired, and fire, police, and safety departments understaffed. 
In towns where the Commonwealth takes land off local tax rolls, it provides payments in lieu of taxes – or PILOTs. In FY26, Shutesbury received a PILOT of $299,392 for the 4,979 acres of the town held by the Commonwealth. That’s 4 percent of the town’s FY26 budget revenue in exchange for 30 percent of its land and comes to just $60.13 per acre.  
Statewide, by contrast, the average PILOT is about $130 per acre. 
Every Quabbin town suffers this disparity. Pelham, for example, gives up 35 percent of its land for the reservoir and gets $56.59 per acre. Hardwick gives up 20 percent and gets $26.24 per acre. New Salem gives up 91 percent for just $21.21 per acre. 
Shutesbury’s Quabbin land has the potential to generate tax revenue of $510 per acre. That means its PILOT of $60.13 per acre is just 11.8 percent of the land’s actual tax value. In FY26 alone, then, Shutesbury was forced to forgo revenue of up to $3.1 million because of Quabbin. In FY26, the 12 Quabbin watershed towns altogether gave up a total of $54.5 million in potential tax revenue because of Quabbin and received just PILOTs of just $3.2 million, or 6 percent of that land’s tax value—a loss of $51.3 million. 
And while the actual tax value of this land has increased exponentially over the past five years, the amount of the Quabbin PILOTs has not. Between FY21 and FY26, the total budget for the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority has increased $128.3 million (16.2 percent) while the amount set aside from that budget for PILOTs to the 12 Quabbin towns has increased just $111,597 (3.6 percent). The portion of the MWRA budget set aside for Quabbin PILOTs has in fact gone down over those five years, from 0.39 percent in FY21 to 0.35 percent in FY26. 
The state’s PILOT system treats Quabbin land as nearly worthless. In reality, Quabbin land is the most valuable land in Massachusetts, because without it, more than 2.7 million people in 53 communities throughout Eastern Massachusetts — 40 percent of the state’s population — would have no water. 
If Shutesbury’s Quabbin land were developed to the same density as the rest of town, it would generate enough tax revenue to pay 37 percent of the town budget. Assuming a proportional increase in service costs if the Quabbin land were developed to the same density as the rest of the town currently, that means every Shutesbury homeowner pays roughly 32 percent more in property taxes because of the reservoir. 
The average Shutesbury homeowner paid approximately $2,100 more in property taxes last year than they would have if the Quabbin did not exist. For comparison, the average single-family Boston water bill in FY26 was $1,300. Like all the Quabbin towns, Shutesbury is, through those higher property taxes, subsidizing the true cost of the water used by its eastern neighbors.
Like their neighbors to the east, Quabbin watershed residents pay a price for Quabbin water; unlike their neighbors to the east, Quabbin watershed residents do not get to drink that water—even as household and public wells go dry or are contaminated by PFAS, as fire departments run out of water to fight fires, as school playgrounds and athletic fields are closed for the year due to a lack of irrigation water, and as water bans are put into place across the region. The engine and lifeblood of Eastern Massachusetts’s economic life, and actual life, is Quabbin water, but that water flows east at the literal expense of those who provide and protect it. 
When the Quabbin host communities, their legislators, citizens, and supporters talk about Quabbin equity, they are talking about the state’s obligation to make those communities whole. They are talking about the moral imperative the Commonwealth has to bring Quabbin towns’ finances in line with comparable communities across the state by offsetting a fair portion of the cost burden imposed on them by the presence of the reservoir.  
This would mean helping them achieve solvency, stability, and the ability to maintain schools, roads, emergency services, and other basic services—including the very conservation, emergency, and land use regulation services that keep Quabbin safe, guarding the groundwater, aquifer, and ecological context that supplies Eastern Massachusetts with clean water every single day. 
Nobody expects the state to compensate the Quabbin communities for 100 percent of the tax value of the land the Commonwealth has taken from those towns—there is a public-good value in that land’s use for water supply, carbon sequestration, conservation, and recreation. But, based on the tremendous revenues the Quabbin generates annually and the essential role Quabbin water plays in the life of Eastern Massachusetts, it is clear that 6 percent of the land’s tax value is far too low a payment. 
In the 1930s, when the Swift River Valley was flooded to make Quabbin, the people of Enfield, Greenwich, Prescott, Dana, and other smaller villages surrendered homes, farms, businesses, and communities for the good of the Commonwealth. Those towns no longer exist, but 88 years later, the towns surrounding Quabbin continue to sacrifice for the reservoir and everyone it serves. It is time for the Commonwealth to recognize and remedy that sacrifice.  
The Massachusetts residents of the Quabbin communities are not asking for charity. They are asking for equity. Because while Boston drinks their water, they drown in the ever-increasing tax burden that stems directly from an inequitable PILOT system.  
In 1927, The New York Times reported on the plan to dismantle the four Quabbin towns, observing, “Greater Boston by no means is indifferent to the tragedy which the need of the city inflicts upon these innocent bystanders.”  
Those who live in the remaining Quabbin towns hope that their neighbors in Greater Boston, including the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority, Gov. Healey, and the state legislators from the 53 communities who depend on Quabbin water, remain “by no means indifferent” to their continuing suffering. 
Matteo Pangallo is the land use clerk for the Town of Shutesbury and chair of the town’s Community Preservation Committee.

title: Vermont keeps a list of where large crowds gather. The feds get a copy.
description:
For nearly a decade, the state has quietly compiled the list of large public gatherings. Town clerks are just now finding out about it.  
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont keeps a list of where large crowds gather. The feds get a copy..
text:
Thousands of people participate in a Fourth of July parade in Warren on Saturday, July 4, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
State and federal authorities looking for potential threats have long monitored parades, sporting events and county fairs in Vermont — and some town officials are only now finding out. 
Last week, town clerks throughout Vermont received an email asking if they would voluntarily hand over a list of potential public and private events of at least 2,500 attendees in their respective towns. Susan Gage, Brandon’s town clerk and treasurer, had never heard of such a request in her 12-year tenure.
The email came from the Vermont Homeland Security Unit, a state entity under Vermont State Police that’s fully funded by the federal government. The unit facilitates something called the Vermont Intelligence Center, which describes as its goal identifying signs of criminal and terrorism-related activity in the state.    
“I suppose we just had a little fair in town, and if something horrible happened there, I would hope that there would be people that would respond quickly,” Gage said in an interview with VTDigger. “But at the same time … we don’t need monitoring.”
Gage turned down the state’s request.
“I can’t help but wonder about the motivations or ‘masked’ incentives in this request,” she responded to Paul Locke, the Vermont Homeland Security Unit’s program planner, in an email she shared with VTDigger.
Lia Ernst, legal director at the American Civil Liberties Union of Vermont, similarly had questions about how the information is stored and shared. 
“When assessing whether these kinds of practices and data collection present a risk to people’s civil liberties, we would wonder what specific criteria law enforcement officials are using to assess whether an event is ‘high-risk’ or not, what tactics may be put into motion when an event is designated as such, and what safeguards are in place to ensure officials are not inhibiting people’s First Amendment rights through their actions,” she wrote in an email to VTDigger.
The state homeland security unit’s annual request is part of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s Special Event Assessment Rating program, also known as SEAR. 
Vermont is required as part of the program to compile the list each year and forward it to the federal government, which rates the special events on a scale depending on if they meet certain criteria, such as national or international importance, potential threats to public safety and level of media attention. However, the towns have a choice of whether they want to contribute.  
Using the list, the state homeland security unit can know when to prepare local and state law enforcement to assemble at events ahead of time, including concerts, parades, county fairs, marathons, firework displays, sporting events and holiday gatherings with at least 2,500 people, according to a special events form listed on the unit’s website. 
While the list monitors the time and place of the events, the attendees themselves are not logged. The special events reporting form also asks for the event sponsors, any additional security controls, the expected number of attendees and whether a special events permit has been filed with state police. 
Vermont’s participation in the program has been ongoing since 2007, Director of the Vermont Homeland Security Unit Ronald LaFond wrote in an email to VTDigger. 
The exact level of needed support and resources from federal partners, along with coordination between state and federal law enforcement, is determined by a formal risk classification, according to LaFond. 
In the past, the state’s events have never triggered the deployment of federal resources, LaFond wrote, adding that the state’s events “have limited national impact.” 
“This program adds to the overall resilience of every community and helps local first responders and state public safety organizations have an overall view of large scale events in the state to better protect the citizens and guests of Vermont,” LaFond wrote.
A precedent for monitoring
In 2025, the Vermont Intelligence Center compiled a statewide directory of events that attracted at least 1,000 people, according to the Vermont Homeland Security Unit’s website. The request was only sent to emergency services, such as local fire and police departments. 
This year, however, the outreach for the list was expanded to town officials after a lack of input statewide from emergency services in previous years, Kenneth A. Deschaine, the Vermont Intelligence Center’s counter-terrorism and critical infrastructure analyst, wrote in an email to Gage that she provided to VTDigger. 
LaFond noted that Vermont was not doing anything unusual in relation to the program, as their efforts are similar to those seen nationwide. 
The list itself, he added, is maintained by the VIC for no longer than one year after the submission. 
Gage, the Brandon town clerk, acknowledges that what she called her “paranoia” about the program — unfounded or otherwise — comes partly in light of her disapproval of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s presence in the nation, much less Vermont. 
After getting the email, Gage made an effort to reach out to several other town clerks to see if they had also received it. Some shared similar concerns as she did though not to the same degree, she noted. 
Had the request been one town officials knew of in past years, Gage continued, she would not have been as alarmed. 
“That’s the kind of emotions I think that are evoked now when our government is militarized against its citizens and its citizens’ neighbors,” Gage said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: The age-old debate of election access vs. security is at center of current national debate
description: A voter marks his ballot during Democratic and Repulican presidential primary elections, as well as for U.S. Senate and U.S. House of Representatives at Precinct 27, the Grove Park Community Center in Jackson, Tuesday, March 12, 2024
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
British jurist William Blackstone is cited with establishing the principle dating back to the 1700s that it is better for 10 guilty people to go free than one innocent person be incarcerated.
That principle continues to be cited and debated. The debate even questions what would be the appropriate number of guilty people going free opposed to one innocent person suffering a conviction and punishment.
A version of that principle also is at the center of a national debate about voting.
Some politicians, led by Republican President Donald Trump, and backed by Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves, contend that the federal Congress should impose national voting standards that would reduce the chances of election fraud.
Other politicians, primarily Democrats, say instances of voting fraud are rare, and studies seem to support that argument, while changes proposed by Trump could make it difficult for eligible voters to cast a ballot.
Hence, the argument seems to be whether preventing what appears to be a few instances of voter fraud is more important than election access. How many people should be denied or hindered in their right to vote to prevent rare occurrences of voter fraud?
Mississippi politicians have a long – and sometimes sordid – history of siding with the argument that preventing voter fraud is more important than ensuring easy voter access.
Even today, it is more difficult to vote by mail in Mississippi than in any state in the nation. In many cases, people voting by mail must have their signature notarized at two steps in the process.
Other states have found what appears to be a more efficient and user friendly way to vote by mail while still ensuring voter security.
In many states, for instance, people voting by mail must provide the last four digits of their Social Security number or a state-issued voter identification number on the ballot. In other states, ballots received in the mail undergo an intense signature verification process, and importantly, normally there are election observers from the political parties who can challenge the ballots.
For decades, Republicans in Mississippi sought a voter identification requirement. Democrats, particularly Black Democrats, tried to block the efforts, arguing older African Americans who were denied the right to vote, would view a voter identification requirement as a return to the old days of Jim Crow.
Republicans in the Mississippi Legislature were offered a compromise that elderly voters – born before a certain date – would be exempt from having an identification to vote. Even though that provision ultimately would have led to a time when all people would have had to show an ID to vote, Republicans rejected the proposal and instead placed on the ballot a citizen-sponsored initiative requiring people to have a government-issued photo identification to vote.
That measure overwhelmingly passed in 2011.
Republican Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann presides over the Senate in a special legislative session at the Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, July 15, 2026.  Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi Today
Despite the argument that a requirement of a government-issued photo ID would restrict election access, it could be argued this was an instance when Mississippi politicians made efforts to ensure people were not denied their rights.
Then Secretary of State Delbert Hosemann, who now serves as lieutenant governor, was charged with enacting the new voting requirement. To his credit, Hosemann took his job seriously and developed a plan to ensure all Mississippians had relatively easy access to a government ID and ensured multiple types of identification could be presented to vote.
For instance, it was determined that in Mississippi a student identification could be presented to vote. Texas, on the other hand, prevents student IDs from being used to vote, but allows gun licenses to be used.
The Texas law faced legal challenges. Hosemann likes to brag that the Mississippi law was not even challenged in court. 
President Trump wants to greatly limit voting by mail while requiring an identification to vote.
The fact of the matter is that most states – 36 – require an identification to vote. And even the president’s home state of Florida allows voting by mail – a process he often takes advantage of by voting by mail while he rails against it
So, perhaps the question is whether voter security is more important than ballot access for some people but not for others?
That like, Blackstone’s original premise, is an age-old debate.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Immigrants helped shape Arkansas. The state shouldn’t forget that history.
description: I’ve never been to Tontitown, nor have I had the pleasure of partaking in its storied annual Grape Festival. But the northwest Arkansas community founded by Italian immigrants feels familiar to me. That’s partly because of Deputy Editor Antoinette Grajeda’s recent article on how the debate over immigration enforcement is playing out in the small […]
text:
Taken between 1899-1900, this photo shows the first class of students who attended a one-room school for Italian immigrants in Tontitown, Arkansas. (Tontitown Historical Museum courtesy of the Basitanelli Collection)I’ve never been to Tontitown, nor have I had the pleasure of partaking in its storied annual Grape Festival. But the northwest Arkansas community founded by Italian immigrants feels familiar to me.
That’s partly because of Deputy Editor Antoinette Grajeda’s recent article on how the debate over immigration enforcement is playing out in the small northwest Arkansas community. 
Reading about Tontitown reminded me of Hibbing, the Minnesota mining town where my grandfather and father were raised. Just like Tontitown, Hibbing was founded in the late 19th century and its identity was shaped by the immigrants who settled there to make a better life for themselves.
There are places like Tontitown and Hibbing all over this country, places whose histories are interwoven with immigration. They’re proof of how immigration has shaped the country from its beginnings. That lesson needs to be repeated in the face of increasingly hostile anti-immigrant rhetoric.
In Arkansas, that climate goes against the history of a state that has relied on immigrants. Some of the state’s most well-known communities and traditions exist because earlier generations chose to welcome immigrants rather than shun them.



Let us know what you think...


 


Tontitown is just one of several communities founded by immigrants that are part of this story. Several enclaves that can trace their roots to Italian immigration can be found in the state. They include Sunnyside Plantation in the Delta region where Tontitown’s founders first settled before moving to northwest Arkansas. Just outside Little Rock is the tiny community of Little Italy, which traces its history to the early 1900s.
Arkansas’ history is a constant reminder of the value of immigration, from the founding of Stuttgart as a colony for German migrants in the 1800s to the Latino and Marshallese communities in northwest Arkansas. 
Arkansas has also stood out for the moments it has welcomed people displaced from other countries, as it did in 1975 when former Gov. David Pryor allowed 55,000 Vietnamese refugees to come through Fort Chaffee. Pryor welcomed the first of the refugees with a brass band.
But the state more recently is embarking on a different path that in many ways echoes the anti-immigrant sentiment that people in Tontitown faced when they first moved here. 
That path includes a full-throated endorsement of President Donald Trump’s rhetoric blaming immigrants for crime. And Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ unproven claims linking businesses to communist China.
Given this environment and the nationwide crackdown during Trump’s second term, it’s understandable why Tontitown’s participation in a federal immigration enforcement program has prompted such a backlash. 
The embrace of anti-immigrant policies and rhetoric even bucks the state’s most recent history, especially from Republican leaders. 
As Arkansas governor, Sanders’ father Mike Huckabee spoke out forcefully against legislation targeting unauthorized immigrants. The Republican governor and Baptist minister quipped that a lawmaker who proposed denying state services to immigrants in the country illegally “drinks a different kind of Jesus juice.” Huckabee once struck a welcoming tone toward immigrants that contrasted sharply with Trump’s.
“Every night, I get on my knees and thank God I’m in a country people are trying to break into, rather than one they’re trying to break out of,” Huckabee said during his presidential bid in 2015.
And Sanders’ predecessor, former Gov. Asa Hutchinson, appeared before lawmakers to defend his decision to continue accepting new refugees, addressing skepticism from some fellow Republicans.
“If we say no to them, then we lose the talent, the entrepreneurship, and humanity of those who love America. Yes, they can go elsewhere, but Arkansas will benefit from their presence,” he said in 2020.
History shows that a welcoming attitude toward immigrants and those seeking refuge is what helped make Arkansas great. It can again. Remembering that history is a good start.

title: More than $50 million available in new rural health grants
description: Applications are open for a new wave of $50.5 million in Rural Health Transformation Program grants through the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services. New grants are available across an array of topic areas including childcare for rural healthcare workers, technology support and equipment and technology upgrades for rural ambulance services. “[...]
text:
Interim Health and Human Services Commissioner Pat Traynor speaks next to Gov. Kelly Armstrong during a 2025 press conference. (Mary Steurer/North Dakota Monitor)Applications are open for a new wave of $50.5 million in Rural Health Transformation Program grants through the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services.
New grants are available across an array of topic areas including childcare for rural healthcare workers, technology support and equipment and technology upgrades for rural ambulance services.
“These funding opportunities give communities the flexibility to invest in what they need most, whether that’s supporting healthcare workers, improving access to care, promoting healthier lifestyles or using technology in new ways,” interim HHS Commissioner Pat Traynor said in a Thursday news release.
The new grants and application deadlines are:

Supporting statewide behavioral health needs assessments and training for parents and caregivers to better support behavioral health. One grant for $500,000. Due Aug. 8.
Equipment and technology grants to strengthen rural ambulance services. About $22 million in total funding. About 110 grants of $200,000 each. Due Aug. 9.
Childcare solutions to recruit and retain rural healthcare workers. About $3 million in total funding. Thirty-eight grants of about $78,000 each. Due Aug. 11.
Remote patient monitoring technology to assist patient access to home care. About $1.6 million in total funding. Twenty grants of about $80,000 each. Due Aug. 14.
Telehealth infrastructure grants for rural and tribal communities. About $3.6 million in total funding. Twenty-five grants of about $144,000 each. Due Aug. 14.
Technology support to reduce reliance on in-person rural healthcare staff. About $5 million in total funding. Twenty grants averaging $250,000 each. Due Aug. 18.

“Every community faces different challenges, so there isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution to improving rural health,” Traynor said.
North Dakota officials celebrate being among big winners in federal rural health funding

Information about an additional $2 million in grant funding to buy accessible vehicles to serve rural residents, including Medicaid recipients, and non-emergency appointments is expected to be announced in coming weeks, the department said. Those grants will have four recipients with an average award of about $500,000 each.
The department said applicants may apply for more than one grant. Additional information, eligibility requirements and application materials can be found through the HHS website.
The new grants are part of North Dakota’s nearly $200 million first year allotment to strengthen rural healthcare as part of the One, Big Beautiful Bill Act signed into law by President Donald Trump in 2025.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont’s fiscal success rests on foundation laid by Malloy, others
description: Former Gov. Dannel P. Malloy and legislators who served with him ordered tax hikes that generated billions for CT during Ned Lamont's tenure.
text:
Central to Gov. Ned Lamont’s political brand and his run for a rare third term is a fiscal discipline that has contributed to Connecticut’s extraordinary run of budget surpluses.
He’s wrapped seven consecutive years in the black, using $11 billion of those unspent funds to wipe out pension debt. No other governor in modern history has made one such payment.
And Lamont, a Democrat who has served with strong Democratic legislative majorities, cut state income tax rates in 2023, something done only once before in the 35-year history of the levy, while still building a record-setting budget reserve that tops $4.4 billion.
But the governor owes some of his success to hard things done prior to his election in 2018, much of it by Dannel P. Malloy, the Democratic predecessor who left office with one of the lowest gubernatorial approval ratings in the U.S.
Malloy and the legislators who served with him between 2011 and 2018 ordered two major tax hikes — centered on Connecticut’s wealthy — that have generated billions for the state’s coffers throughout Lamont’s administration.
Malloy used reports, contract negotiations and a cross-state promotional tour to force a new fiscal culture and end the longstanding practice of inflating pension costs while pushing them onto future generations.
Lawmakers from both parties wrote aggressive budget caps in 2017, when Republicans held half the seats in the Senate. One of them limited how revenue spikes from volatile sources could be used, a favorite tool employed Lamont, who has insisted that increased spending be matched by sustainable revenue growth.
Governors who took CT’s pension debt very seriously
“I think I’m the only governor — ever — to take our pension obligations seriously and make a difference there,” Lamont said in June 2025, shortly before wrapping the annual budget cycle with nearly $1.3 billion unspent and available to reduce pension debt.
Over the past seven years, Lamont has dedicated an average of nearly $1.6 billion in surplus to offset Connecticut’s unfunded pension obligations, a burden that still exceeds $30 billion and likely won’t be paid off until well into the 2040s.
But without all those extra deposits, the required contributions that already consume a hefty chunk of the state budget would be $800 million to $900 million greater each year.
“I think people are taking a second look at Connecticut” because of this fiscal dedication, Lamont said this week. “They say, ‘They’ve got their act together.’”
By comparison, governors and legislatures for decades prior to 2011 had forfeited billions of dollars in potential investment earnings by not properly saving for benefits pledged to state employees and teachers.
But it wasn’t Lamont’s successes that left some observers stunned by his claim of exclusive dedication to sound fiscal management of pensions.
That’s because some important things happened after the decades of pension mismanagement — but before Lamont became governor.

Dannel P. Malloy and Ned Lamont, the governor and governor-elect at the time, in December 2018. Credit: ctmirror.org

Despite inheriting the largest projected deficit in state history — a $3.7 billion gap equal to almost one-fifth of the General Fund — new Gov. Malloy took office in 2011 and drew his own line in the pension sand.
The Stamford Democrat tore up contracts that had allowed his predecessors to easily short-change required pension contributions and leave the mess for future generations to clean.
By Malloy’s second year, annual pension expenses were almost 70% greater than pre-recession levels, further straining a budget that already had lost close to $2 billion in yearly revenue due to a sagging economy.
He twice negotiated wage freezes and benefit givebacks from unions, shrank the Executive Branch workforce by 10% and signed two of the largest tax hikes in state history, frustrating not just his labor base but much of the electorate.
Malloy crisscrossed the state during his first few months in office, holding 17 town meetings to explain the fiscal ticking time bomb represented by unfunded pension obligations. Four years later, he commissioned a report from the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College, which traced the state’s poor savings habits back to 1939.
Malloy, who generally has avoided commenting on election-year politics since becoming the chancellor of the University of Maine, declined to be interviewed for this story.
“He took an issue that was [behind] closed doors … and really put it out there for people to understand the level of the problem,” said Joe Aresimowicz, the House speaker during the last two years of Malloy’s tenure and first two of Lamont’s.
“It takes a different kind of human being to stand up in front of hundreds of people night after night, knowing that they disagree with you, knowing that they’re angry, knowing that they’re going to yell at you, and you keep doing it anyway,” said Roy Occhiogrosso, a senior adviser and campaign strategist for Malloy. “And it was because he believed deeply that you cannot fix the massive problems that he inherited unless you educate people about them first.”
Legislative proposals to defer pension contributions, a common sight during challenging fiscal times, were a thing of the past by the time Lamont took office in January 2019.
“In Dan Malloy’s defense, he was the first guy to at least make the current [pension] payments,” the governor said, “and I respect him for that.”

Former Gov. Dannel P. Malloy shakes hands with Susan Johnson in 2011 after announcing a budget deal that raises the income and sales taxes but avoids tax increases that Malloy proposed previously. Credit: Mark Mirko / Hartford Courant

Malloy’s tax hikes forced high earners to pay more
Even so, Lamont notes that state finances weren’t entirely rosy when he took over for Malloy.
Nonpartisan analysts projected the budget, unless adjusted, was on pace for a nearly $2 billion deficit, a 10% gap, unless adjustments were made.
But Malloy, who had inherited no rainy day fund and $1 billion in operating debt to pay off, left $1.2 billion in the budget reserve for Lamont and no IOUs to cover.
Lamont ultimately closed his deficit by raising some business taxes and by canceling some sales tax exemptions and previously approved tax cuts that hadn’t taken effect yet. He was spared from increasing the state income tax, which carried the biggest political risk.
A key reason for that, though, was the income tax hikes Malloy signed into law, measures he used to reshape Connecticut’s tax structure significantly.
Enacted in 1991, the income tax largely was flat at the onset. All filers and their earnings initially were taxed at 4.5%, though legislators built in some personal exemptions to ease burdens somewhat on lower-income households.
Even after the 1995 legislature created a new credit to offset a portion of local property taxes paid by the middle class, that group and the wealthy both paid very similar effective rates for most of the income tax’s first two decades.
But under Malloy, it evolved into a seven-tiered system, with rates ranging from 3% to 6.99%. Different portions of a filer’s earnings would be taxed at different rates, with higher percentages applied as income increased.
Connecticut also established a “recapture” system that ensured the wealthiest filers didn’t fully benefit from the lower rates and paid close to 6.99% on all their income.
The income tax became far more progressive under Malloy, meaning the effective rate grew along with a filer’s ability to pay. But it also became a more powerful revenue engine for Connecticut.
The stock market has enjoyed robust growth during Lamont’s tenure, especially since the COVID pandemic, and those higher rates have allowed his administration to take maximum advantage of the surge.
Quarterly income tax receipts, which are tied heavily to the investment earnings of Connecticut’s wealthiest, are estimated to have topped $4.3 billion last fiscal year, which ended June 30. That’s up almost 40% in just five years.
“Ned Lamont thinks that the reason Connecticut is in good fiscal shape is because of him,” said Rep. Josh Elliott of Hamden, who is challenging Lamont in an Aug. 11 primary for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination.
But the hard work of raising revenue “was all done before him,” Elliott added.
The Republican gubernatorial nominee, Sen. Ryan Fazio of Greenwich, said the key to Lamont’s fiscal track record stems from steps lawmakers took nine years ago, when Republicans had more seats and more influence.

Legislative leaders share a light moment as they announce a budget deal in 2018. From left, Senate Republican leader Len Fasano, Senate President Pro Tem Martin Looney, House Minority Leader Themis Klarides, Senate Majority leader Bob Duff and House Majority Leader Matt Ritter. Behind Klarides is House Speaker Joe Aresimowicz. Credit: Clarice Silber / CTMirror.org

After a Democratic majority failed to enact a new budget despite nine months of negotiations in 2017, minority Republicans were brought into the talks. The final compromise included strict new budget caps that have helped generate unprecedented surpluses averaging more than 8% of the annual budget.
In the two decades prior to these caps, the annual budget closed, on average, 1/10th of 1% in the black.
“I think Democrats would agree those [fiscal] guardrails would never have been in play but for the Republicans’ insistence on them,” said House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford.
“I thought the [2017] guardrails made some sense,” Lamont said, “and I’m glad they did it.”
Fazio added Lamont has been more focused in recent years working around these caps to spend more.
“The governor inherited the most important and better economic policy in Connecticut in my lifetime,” Fazio said, “and after eight years in office has virtually destroyed them.” 
Lamont and majority Democrats in the General Assembly did compromise in May and shift more than $800 million from a mandatory savings program into the General Fund.
Still, Fazio’s claim that the budget caps are effectively nullified is debatable, at best. 
The governor notes much of that was done to accommodate key investments to help low- and middle-income families. The new state budget sends $280 million extra in grants to cities and towns this fiscal year while depositing more than $410 million into a new trust to expand affordable childcare.
And even with those investments, Connecticut will reduce its unfunded pension obligations this year by a level that nearly matches prior supplemental debt payments Lamont has made.
In fact, Elliott’s challenge is based in large part on his argument that Lamont has been too tight-fisted.
And while Elliott supports raising taxes more on Connecticut’s wealthy to finance tax relief for the middle class, the governor says the income tax rate cuts and other changes he signed in 2023 already save those households $300 to $400 per year.

Then-Gov. Dannel P. Malloy, left, greets Connecticut’s then-governor-elect Ned Lamont at the Governor’s Residence in Hartford, Conn., Thursday, Nov. 8,  2018.  Credit: Jessica Hill / AP

Lamont: Saving money requires more than budget caps
Connecticut’s coffers have swelled before, thanks to economic booms and budgetary spending caps. But before Lamont, that didn’t translate into billions removed from state debt totals.
In other words, the governor said, leadership is necessary, too.
“I have to remind people every day how dire our circumstance was” in decades past, Lamont said. “Today we’re in a very different place.”
The governor added that “We had a spending cap going back to the early ’90s, and everyone winked at it.”
For example, Republican governors and Democratic-controlled legislatures ran up $3.6 billion in potential surpluses between 2003 and 2008, according to records from the comptroller’s office and the legislature’s nonpartisan Office of Fiscal Analysis.
Almost two-thirds of it was spent.
Aresimowicz added that while he’s very proud of the reforms lawmakers enacted in 2017, Lamont’s “firm belief that we have to stick with it” was a driving factor behind the state’s greatly improved financial standing.
“Malloy set the foundation for it, made the public more aware and the legislators more aware,” the former speaker said. But “in the absence of Gov. Ned Lamont, I don’t know that we would have gotten to the place we are now.”
CT Mirror Capitol Bureau Chief Mark Pazniokas contributed to this story.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: A decade after Obama’s historic Hiroshima trip, the world edges toward oblivion. Can we step away?
description: Thursday is the 81st anniversary of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, and as a society we’re still struggling with how to respond to the ability to annihilate ourselves. Ten years ago, Barack Obama became the first sitting U.S. president to visit Hiroshima, and his message was one of reflection. He spoke of the 100,000 Japanese […]
text:
The A Bomb Dome overlooks Hiroshima in 2015. The dome, which was part of the city's industrial exhibition hall, was directly beneath the atomic bomb dropped pm Aug. 6, 1945. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)Thursday is the 81st anniversary of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, and as a society we’re still struggling with how to respond to the ability to annihilate ourselves.
Ten years ago, Barack Obama became the first sitting U.S. president to visit Hiroshima, and his message was one of reflection. He spoke of the 100,000 Japanese men, women, and children who died in the Aug. 6, 1945, blast, along with thousands of Koreans and the dozen American prisoners of war.
“Their souls speak to us,” Obama said alongside Prime Minister Shinzo Abe at the Hiroshima Peace Memorial. “They ask us to look inward, to take stock of who we are and what we might become.”
When Obama delivered those remarks on May 2016, he had less than a year remaining in his last term in office. Already the world was beginning to change. Donald Trump had won the Indiana GOP presidential primary and, despite expectations, had become the party’s presumptive nominee. Sanctions against Iran were lifted after the U.N. certified the country had sufficiently dismantled its nuclear weapons program, as called for by a landmark agreement. In June 2016, the United Kingdom would narrowly vote to leave the European Union, foreshadowing the right-wing populism that would soon sweep western democracies.
The year before Obama visited Hiroshima, I was there, to speak at the annual peace conference. At the conference I talked about meeting atomic photographer Yoshito Matsushige in Hiroshima decades before, when I was a young newspaper reporter from Kansas. Matsushige was among the dozens of hibakusha, or Japanese A-bomb survivors, I had interviewed about their horrific experiences, which many described as “beyond imagination.”
During the conference, I met Yasuyoshi Komizo, chair of the Hiroshima Peace Culture Foundation and secretary-general of Mayors for Peace. Pondering this year’s anniversary, I asked Komizo, who has since retired but remains a peace activist, his thoughts on Obama’s speech and how much closer the world has come to disaster since 2016.
Komizo told me in an email interview there was general optimism after Obama, in his 2009 Prague speech, announced “America’s commitment to seek the peace and security of a world without nuclear weapons.”
The hope that Obama would visit Hiroshima was realized seven years later, in the midst of a turbulent presidential election year, and despite his advisers urging caution.
“He was under immense public pressure within the U.S. not to offer an apology to Japan,” Komizo said.
Obama did not apologize, but in Hiroshima he talked about the shared responsibility “to curb such sufferings again.” He expressed hope for choosing a future in which Hiroshima and Nagasaki are known “as the start of our moral awakening.”
After Obama concluded his remarks, he approached Sunao Tsuboi, a hibakusha, teacher, and co-chair of Nihon Hidankyō, the atomic bomb survivors organization that would be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2024 for its efforts to create a world free of nuclear weapons.
“Tsuboi welcomed Obama with open arms,” Komizo said of the literal embrace that followed, “knowing Obama (was) doing his best but also bound by limitations. We cannot say that there are no bitter feelings in the hearts of the hibakusha, but I think Tsuboi found sincerity in Obama as a leader.”
Obama also greeted Shigeaki Mori, another hibakusha, and expressed his gratitude for Mori’s efforts to track down the stories of the American prisoners of war who were killed by the bombing and to find their families.
At the atomic bomb museum, Komizo said, Obama looked at the various displays and artifacts and paused at a painting by Ikuo Hirayama, a Japanese artist known for his dream-like silk road desert landscapes. Komizo said he told the president that Hirayama, who died in 2009, had been a Hiroshima atomic bomb survivor. Hirayama created only one painting about the bombing, “The Holocaust of Hiroshima,” in the hope atomic weapons would never be used again. Obama thanked him for the information, Komizo recalled, and then became reflective.
I recall looking at the same silk road painting in the peace museum and being oddly moved, although the subject matter has nothing to do with the bombing. The power in Hirayama’s work, beyond its artistry, may be in its juxtaposition with the horrors on display at the museum — a charred tricycle, the blood-stained uniforms of school children, a human shadow etched in stone by the heat of the blast. For every story told by one of the atomic bomb survivors, a thousand were lost.
Chair Yasuyoshi Komizo stands with Cardinal Fernando Filoni in 2017 at the peace museum at Hiroshima, Japan. Komizo is discussing a tricycle scorched by the Aug. 6, 1945, atomic bombing of the city. (Photo by the Hiroshima Peace Culture Foundation)
One of the stories told over and again was by Akihiro Takahashi, who was 14 when the bomb fell on Hiroshima. When I interviewed him in 1986, he was chair of the Peace Culture Foundation, the same post Komizo would assume years later.
On the morning of Aug. 6, 1945, Takahashi and his classmates were lining up on the middle school yard for roll call when they spotted an American B-29 bomber, causing the children to shout “B-san!” They were used to seeing B-29s on their way to bomb other Japanese cities, but so far Hiroshima had been lucky.
The luck ran out that morning.
“I was pointing at the B-29, and two or three teachers came out from the school building,” Takahashi told me through a translator. “The class leader told us to get back in line. I heard a tremendous noise and all of a sudden it was dark.”
When the dust lifted, the school was gone and his classmates were lying motionless around him. He and another boy were alive, but their clothes were in tatters, their skin was burned, and they were bleeding from glass fragments.
“It was a kind of hell,” Takahashi said. “The two of us, we had to crawl over the rubble just like cats or dogs do. To 14-year-old boys, it was a very scary scene.”
They made their way past piles of corpses and other survivors, who walked like ghosts with their flesh hanging from their arms. At the river, Takahashi soothed his wounds in the water for hours until the black rain began, then he started for home. Relatives found him along the way, and he spent a year and a half in a hospital. When I met him, he was 55. His right arm was still small and useless and covered with thick scars, and his right ear was shriveled.
In 1980, during a trip to Washington, D.C., Takahashi met Paul Tibbets, the pilot of the Enola Gay, the B-29 that dropped the atomic bomb that nearly killed him. Takahashi recalled that Tibbets was reluctant to talk to him, because he had never met a survivor before.
“I offered my hand and I said, ‘I have no intention of complaining to you.’ He saw the (scars) on my right hand and asked if the atomic bomb had caused them,” Takahashi said.
He said he told Tibbets that he prayed for the day when nuclear weapons would be abolished. There would be no winners or losers next time, he said, because the entire earth would be consumed.
Tibbets, according to Takahashi, kept repeating that he had no regrets and was just following orders. He said he would do it again.
“But it seems to me that I thought I saw a tear in his eyes,” Takahashi said. “So I thought he was human after all.”
Takahashi said he invited Tibbets to Hiroshima, but that he declined.
When asked about the meeting years later, Tibbets said the story about the tears was “bulls***.” He also said he would have dropped the atomic bomb on Hanoi during the Vietnam War, if ordered. He told another interviewer that he would have done the same to Islamic extremists.
Tibbets died in 2007. He was 92.
Takashi died in 2011. He was 80.
In 2016, Komizo was invited by the National Park Service to participate in the Manhattan Project National Historical Park scholar’s forum. In his remarks, he said: “A key question is what kind of future we aim for. I hope sincerely that in line with the founding spirit of the United States of America, as well as its global leadership in democracy and human rights, the (NPS) exhibition will be organized to inspire visitors to ponder and work out innovative and more humane ways to achieve peace and prosperity.”
It is difficult to imagine such a forum today, when uncomfortable historical facts are the target of a regime attempting to whitewash history. Last year, the Trump administration asked national park visitors to flag exhibits that said “negative” things.
Last week, the administration posted signs outside the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History about supposed “inaccurate information” inside. The museum, according to the administration, was engaged in anti-white rhetoric, transgender activism, and was “insufficiently patriotic,” according to NPR.
Ten years ago, the Doomsday Clock was at three minutes to midnight.
Since 1947, the clock has been a graphical representation of global catastrophe, as estimated by the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. The farthest the hands have been away from midnight was in 1991, at the end of the cold war, at 17 minutes. In 2016, the clock was at three minutes to midnight.
But in 2020, the Bulletin stopped measuring the risk in minutes. They turned to seconds. In addition to the threat of nuclear war, there was the additional risk posed by climate change, and world leaders had allowed the international political infrastructure for managing threats to erode. By 2024, disruptive technologies such as AI were included in the assessment.
Now, the clock is at 85 seconds to midnight, closer than ever to doomsday.
“A year ago, we warned that the world was perilously close to global disaster and that any delay in reversing course increased the probability of catastrophe,” the Bulletin announced in January 2026. “Rather than heed this warning, Russia, China, the United States, and other major countries have instead become increasingly aggressive, adversarial, and nationalist.”
The turn to global violence did not spare Abe, the prime minister who spoke alongside Obama a decade ago. A divisive figure in Japan, he was assassinated in 2022 by a politically motivated assailant with a homemade shotgun.
It was part of the unraveling of the political order that had stitched the world together after 1945. Japan, which had been a ruthless colonial force, was remade as a western democracy after the war. It took decades for Japan to acknowledge that many of the Koreans killed in Hiroshima were forced laborers or women who had been enslaved as sex workers by the Imperial Japanese Army. Foremost among the challenges of democracy is dealing with the sins of the past while avoiding catastrophe in the present.
As I write, the Iran ceasefire has collapsed and the United States has launched fresh strikes. The Russian invasion of Ukraine has entered its fourth year and is the largest military conflict in Europe since World War II. American diplomacy, once the model for the world, has suffered an erosion of trust and leverage in this Trumpian era of foreign policy by tweet and grift.
Still, Komizo told me, there are ways for the average American to work for peace. I should note that he is careful to avoid disparaging any particular leader or political party, and that his advocacy for peace is based on a nonpartisan humanitarian philosophy.
“Ways to contribute to a nuclear weapons-free world can be manyfold,” he said. “They include arts, music, movies, literature, seminars, exhibitions, education, scientific research, dialogue with politicians. Please be innovative and suit your own skills and tastes.”
Cultivating human bonds is a collaborative effort, he said.
“Such efforts can transcend national boundaries and differences in skin color, religion, gender and generations,” Komizo said. “When people in different backgrounds work together, beyond their seeming differences, they may discover far greater commonality as members of the same human family.”
It will take courage, he said, to build a new foundation on which true peace and security can be built. Although the world has become more challenging in the 10 years since Obama’s visit, Komizo said, he remains optimistic.
“More and more young people are taking to heart the earnest wish for peace of the hibakusha,” he said. “A pulse for peace transcending generations can be heard.”
I hope my friend Komizo is right.
But all I can hear at the moment is my own heart, beating down the seconds.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s $1.6 billion railroad promise
description: It would be nice if officialdom would stop overpromising and under-delivering.
text:
The Connecticut Department of Transportation and state and federal elected officials tried to make some “big news” about our trains last week.  Here’s how most media summarized the story:  “Connecticut has broken ground on the $1.6 billion TIME-1 upgrade of the New Haven Line, targeting speeds of up to 90 mph, improving service by 2035.”



Maybe you saw the media coverage and said “Wow.  Great news.” Or maybe you had a sense of déjà vu and asked yourself two questions:  “Haven’t I heard this promise before?” (Yes) and “Should I believe this promise, delivered in an election year?” (No).
As a journalist I was disappointed (but not surprised) that almost no media asked those same questions, instead just regurgitating the press release.  So let me try to separate the facts from the hype.
Time for CT Project: Your sense of déjà vu was correct as we heard this same announcement five years ago.  And the promises then have yet to be delivered. 
In fact it was in 2019 that commuters were promised a 30-minute train ride from New Haven to Stamford. The fastest trains today are the early morning super-expresses which run non-stop in 45 minutes.  Better, but not what was promised.
Will this really cost $1.6 billion? Yes, and it’s not yet fully funded.  There’s money so far only for Phase One, just $340 million, to rebuild the catenary, fix one bridge and upgrade tracks and signaling.  And this Phase One covers merely three miles of track.
Phases Two and Three, which bring the biggest improvements, are not yet funded. Transportation money from the current White House is drying up, so the prospect of the additional $1.3 billion that’s needed seems to me like wishful thinking.  In the tech world they call such claims “vapor-ware.”
So why announce a project that won’t be finished for nine years when funding is still uncertain?  Because it’s an election year.
Don’t get me wrong.  This work is necessary and decades overdue.  It will make the railroad safer and maybe even faster… assuming the money is found and the work gets done.  But I predict it will all cost more and take longer than the officials hope… or are willing to admit.
Finished by 2035? This will really take nine years?  Yes, and probably longer.  Consider projects like the Walk Bridge in Norwalk, first announced by then-Governor Malloy in 2014, with construction finally beginning in 2023 with an expected completion now in 2029.  Initial cost estimates of $465 million have since doubled.  I’ve been calling it “the billion dollar bridge” since first writing about it 12 years ago. 

The Walk Bridge is under a repair project that will take another three years. Credit: CDOT

Rebuilding a working railroad is expensive and slow.  If Metro-North could shut down the railroad completely, work would go faster… but that is impossible.  So expect a lot of delays for the next decade.
Speeds of up to 90 mph? This is the promise that most angers me because it’s just not true. It’s just like Amtrak’s claim that its new Acela NextGen runs 165 mph.  Yes… for about 10 miles in New Jersey and a few more in Rhode Island, but not the full trip from Boston to Washington.
And Connecticut’s supposed “90 mph” trains… they’ll achieve that for a three mile straight stretch between Stratford and Bridgeport, but almost nowhere else.  And by the way, the promised improved average speed of 70 mph on Metro-North will be the same speed limit before the Bridgeport and Spuyten Duyvil derailments prompted the FRA (Federal Railroad Administration) to lower the speed limits.  And that was 13 years ago.
Don’t believe the hype.   This project is important and I hope it gets built even if it takes longer and costs more than what’s being promised now.  But as I’ve said for years in my CT Rail Commuter Council days, “Our train service will get worse before it gets better”. 
There will be delays, just as we’ve seen on other CDOT projects (like the Darien train station, now 15 months behind schedule) or the never ending work on I-95, I-91 and I-84.
But can’t the CDOT and their pol bosses at least be honest with us and not over-promise and consistently under-deliver? 
And to my fellow journalists… please stop being stenographers.  Our job isn’t to parrot press releases.  It’s to ask the question on every commuter’s mind: “Will this actually happen?”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: More than 1,000 Georgia Democrats meet to strategize for November election
authors: Craig Nelson, The Current GA, Robin Kemp
description: This story has been republished through a partnership with The Current, an independent, in-depth and investigative journalism website for Coastal Georgia. More than 1,000 Georgia Democrats gathered in Savannah Saturday for a pep rally and strategy session, brandishing their determination to put a Democrat, Keisha Lance Bottoms, into the governor’s seat for t[...]
text:
Amanda Hollowell, a candidate for Georgia’s 1st Congressional District, speaks at the Georgia Democratic Convention in Savannah on Aug. 1, 2026. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for AmericaThis story has been republished through a partnership with The Current, an independent, in-depth and investigative journalism website for Coastal Georgia.
More than 1,000 Georgia Democrats gathered in Savannah Saturday for a pep rally and strategy session, brandishing their determination to put a Democrat, Keisha Lance Bottoms, into the governor’s seat for the first time in a generation and to re-elect Jon Ossoff to the U.S. Senate.
The state Democratic party’s daylong convention kicked off with speeches offering a united message: Winds of change are sweeping Georgia, driven by people fed up with the rising cost of living, job insecurities and anxieties that the American dream is slipping away.
Gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks during the 2026 Georgia Democratic Convention in Savannah on Aug. 1, 2026. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for America
“Something is happening in our state. The country is taking notice. This is our year,” declared Charlie Bailey, chair of the state party. Democrats, he said, are offering solutions.
Bailey set the stage for the crucial task of getting people to the polls this fall, even as he seeks to rebuild the party’s organizing strength. The party’s machinery in many, if not most, of Georgia’s 159 counties has withered, due to how long Democrats have been the minority party and to the influence wielded by voting rights and get-out-the-vote groups affiliated with former Democratic gubernatorial candidate Stacey Abrams in recent years.
The state party announced last week it will staff 30 field offices, 60 full-time field organizers and 100 staffers to coordinate with Democratic candidates from the top of the ballot, other statewide offices and local state lawmakers.
Enthusiasm at the convention was high, despite the absence of Georgia’s two Democratic senators: Ossoff — who is running for another six-year term — and Rev. Raphael Warnock, who won re-election in 2024. Bailey and other party officials cited “scheduling conflicts” as the reason for their absence. Neither Ossoff’s campaign or Warnock’s office responded to requests for comment.
Without their presence, the convention crescendoed into a highly produced headliner event for Bottoms, who won 58 percent of the vote in last spring’s party primary but is treading water financially compared to her billionaire rival Rick Jackson.
Jackson, a health care executive who has never run for elected office, spent more than $107 million of his own money to win the Republican primary. Earlier this week, his campaign announced it had purchased $87 million in advertising to start Saturday. In comparison, Bottom’s campaign committee ended the most recent reporting period on April 30 with $257,336.80 in the bank, having spent $1.2 million, according to campaign contribution disclosure reports on file with the state. Her campaign said it received a $1 million donation from the Democratic Governors Association after her first-round primary victory.
Gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks during a campaign event in Brunswick on July 30, 2026. About 500 people attended the event. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for America
Bottoms spent the last three days touring Coastal Georgia, and on Thursday night in Brunswick, a majority Black town nestled among reliably Republican counties, approximately 500 people turned out to hear her promise to expand Medicaid for Georgia’s working poor adults, help veterans and bring more jobs to the region.
At the convention Saturday, Bottoms said the policies supported by “Slick Rick Jackson,” as she called the health executive, have led to immense human suffering. Under Republican state leaders, working class Georgians have had to drop health care insurance due to rising costs, hospitals have closed due to underfunding and more Georgians are losing jobs because of tariffs and inflation, she said.
Jackson, she reminded the crowd, has given at least $1 million dollars to the Trump campaign as he sought endorsements from the president.
“It is abundantly clear that he will never ever stand up for Georgians against Donald Trump,” she said. “He may be running to be Trump’s favorite governor, but I’m running to be yours.”
Before Bottoms’ took the stage, Jackson’s campaign sent emails to reporters that sought to paint the former Atlanta mayor as a dangerous radical. They pointed to her support for the writings of a progressive political writer backed by members of the far-left wing of the party and to her vows to overhaul Republican policies backed by outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp.
Earlier in the week, Jackson made a campaign stop in Camden County, a largely Republican county, where he spoke to a smaller crowd than the one who turned out for Bottoms in neighboring Glynn.
Bottoms’ message of improving the economic wellbeing for everyday Georgians resonated with the delegates who came to Savannah from all corners of the state.
As they nibbled muffins and eggs at breakfast before the plenary, more than a dozen told The Current that the overriding concern of their neighbors was the rising cost of living and that the Democratic candidates’ economic messages would draw voters to the polls.
Ace Campbell, a retired U.S. Army colonel and the second vice chairman of Muskogee County Democrats, expressed confidence in the party’s chances of winning in November. “The events this morning have been electric. It’s showing that we have a good slate of candidates that are knowledgeable in what they do, and they have the energy,” he said.
Local Democratic leaders, meanwhile, put their marks on the convention from the start.
Chatham County Commissioner Aaron “Adot” Whitely, chair of the Chatham County Democratic Party, welcomed the conventioneers. Rev. Paul Smith, senior pastor of Bethlehem Baptist Church in Savannah and president of the Savannah chapter of the NAACP, delivered an invocation.
Savannah Mayor Van Johnson took the podium after Bailey spoke. “We’re on the edge of something great,” he said in rousing speech, bringing attendees to their feet: “Are we ready to make history? . . . Let’s make things happen.”
Amanda Hollowell, the Democratic candidate for Georgia’s 1st Congressional District, had the floor for a five-minute speech, declaring she was running on a “people first” agenda.
Running against the well-funded Republican candidate Jim Kingston, the son of longtime Coastal Georgia Congressman Jack Kingston and a favorite of the Savannah business establishment, she told the crowd that the area deserved a representative in Congress who was more than his “daddy’s name.”
Candidates pose for a group photo during the 2026 Georgia Democratic Convention in Savannah on Aug. 1, 2026. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for America
Candidates for statewide office emphasized their credentials as public safety professionals, business leaders and advocates for the working class.
Tanya Miller, the Democratic candidate for Attorney General and a former homicide prosecutor, told delegates about her mother, a union worker, made unemployed by corporate greed, and grandmother grew up in the rural South.
Judge Penny Reynolds told the audience that a vote for her as secretary of state would be a vote for equality and Civil Rights. “Georgia does not belong to a few people. Georgia belongs to all of us. The right to vote is an inheritance of generations,” said Reynolds, a longtime lawyer and pastor. “America has always been its best when it provides opportunity to everyone,” she said. “We will fight with faith. We will fight with justice. We will win this thing,” she said.
Ahead of Saturday’s event, the chairman of the Georgia Republican Party derided what he called Democrats’ “out-of-touch agenda.”
“This weekend, Georgia Democrats will gather in Savannah to celebrate the very leaders and policies that have failed Georgia families,” Josh McKoon said in a statement.
“They’re asking Georgians to hand their party power so they can continue pushing their agenda of higher costs, soft-on-crime policies, and divisive social priorities. Georgians have seen what Republican leadership has delivered: stronger economic growth, safer communities, secure elections, and responsible governance.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Lahn advocates for privatized Medicaid, defends attack ad against Sand
description: BRITT — Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn defended his Medicaid stance Saturday at the Hancock County Fair in Britt, expressing a need to continue Gov. Kim Reynolds’ healthcare policy. Lahn said delivering healthcare through the private sector with government oversight is “bipartisan,” saying 42 states including Iowa use managed care organizations[...]
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, left, speaks to voters at the Hancock County Fair in Britt on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kadin Luhmann for Iowa Capital Dispatch)BRITT — Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn defended his Medicaid stance Saturday at the Hancock County Fair in Britt, expressing a need to continue Gov. Kim Reynolds’ healthcare policy.
Lahn said delivering healthcare through the private sector with government oversight is “bipartisan,” saying 42 states including Iowa use managed care organizations, including many Democratic states.
“I don’t think the government would do a good job of delivering healthcare for the people of Iowa,” Lahn said. “I think that the private sector can do a great job delivering this, but the government has to hold them accountable. We have to make sure we’re getting the right care, proper payment, and also I will not allow any of these companies to use AI in denying coverage from people.”
Emma O’Brien, a communications staffer for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, said Lahn wants to continue “failed health care policies.”
“Zach Lahn has spent his career as a political operative trying to kick people off their health insurance,” O’Brien said. “Now, he’s promising to continue Iowa’s failed privatized Medicaid system, spearheaded under Gov. Reynolds, which has led to worse care and higher costs for Iowans.”
Lahn defends ad that Sand called ‘dishonest’
During a town hall in Fort Dodge Monday, Sand railed against an attack ad paid for by the Lahn campaign. The advertisement featured edited clips from KCCI broadcasts, in which anchors say the “auditor’s office took no action” when millions of dollars in state funds went missing.
“The only thing that he ran for six weeks after the general election was an attack on me and my record that was so fundamentally dishonest that the TV station, when they saw their anchor’s words being taken out of context, actually made a news story about the television ad to tell people how dishonest it was,” Sand said.
In 2024, $53 million in court debt payments were misallocated to due a computer error in Iowa’s judicial payment systems. Republican lawmakers criticized Sand, who also serves as state auditor. for failing to alert lawmakers or intervene. Sand 
Sand said in December 2024 the auditor’s office had been in contact with officials from the state judicial branch and Department of Transportation multiple times after being notified of the issue in October 2022, and that the office remained in contact with the judicial branch in conducting internal and independent investigations into the issue. He also said the auditor’s office did not have staff equipped to investigate computer errors.

Lahn argued Saturday the ad is not dishonest, and Sand had the authority to step in and do something.
“They’re not false. He is not doing his job,” Lahn said. “In 2025, his office had the statutory authority to get involved in that, and they didn’t do it. Once they miss their audit, he is statutorily allowed to get involved into that, and at the very least, provide help.”
Lahn calls for expanding ESA program for private schools
Lahn spoke with voters Saturday at the Hancock County Fair, where people told him that some of their biggest concerns involve education in Iowa.
Lahn said he wants to expand the Education Savings Account program, which provides taxpayer funds for private school expenses regardless of family income, while simultaneously improving public schools, saying market-based competition will make both better.
“My job as governor is to make sure we have the number one public schools in the country,” Lahn said. “I just had a superintendent at one of my stops today say to me he wants competition. He welcomes competition. He just needs to be unburdened to compete, and so my job is to find these superintendents who want to compete with innovative models and cut out the red tape, give them innovation waivers and a budget to do it, so they know we’re behind them.
Lahn advocates for local foods in schools
Lahn said he spoke with U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins about wanting to put more locally sourced food in Iowa public schools.
“One of my biggest initiatives is how do we get more food served in public schools that is grown in the state of Iowa,” Lahn said. We need to create a new market for small farmers because a lot of this food that’s being served in public schools is already under a USDA food subsidized program, but only the big guys can get in it.”
Lahn optimistic about potential in blue counties
Lahn was also optimistic about his chances in Democratic Iowa counties, such as Polk and Johnson, where he performed well in the primary election.
“I think if you look at where we overperformed the most in the primary, it was Polk County,” Lahn said. “We had a lot of support, and we also had a lot of young people and a lot of non-primary voters come out to support us because we have a message that’s very different, very Iowa-centric. We want to make Iowa the healthiest place to raise a family, tackle the cancer crisis, clean up our water. These are things that Polk County, Johnson County care about.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: 3 dead, 2 injured in Twin Falls In-N-Out shooting
description: This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Aug. 1, 2026. Three people are dead and two are injured after a shooting Saturday afternoon at the Twin Falls In-N-Out, according to a city spokesperson. Joshua Palmer, Twin Falls’ public information officer, confirmed those numbers, though he said in a text message officials […]
text:
Three people are dead and two are injured after a shooting Saturday afternoon at the Twin Falls In-N-Out, according to a city spokesperson. (Photo by Douglas Sacha/Getty Images)This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Aug. 1, 2026.
Three people are dead and two are injured after a shooting Saturday afternoon at the Twin Falls In-N-Out, according to a city spokesperson.
Joshua Palmer, Twin Falls’ public information officer, confirmed those numbers, though he said in a text message officials “expect that number to be higher” as the investigation and response continues.
Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said in a late afternoon press conference that the suspected shooter is dead “nearby on the scene” and that he believes “the threat to the community is over.”
“We are working to try to ascertain his identity and the motivations behind [the shooting] and we’ll be able to figure that out in the next coming days,” Hicks said.
He shared few details, but called it “a very chaotic scene.”

Idahoans, join me in keeping the Twin Falls community in your prayers as law enforcement and first responders respond to an active shooter situation near In-N-Out.
Please avoid the area and follow directions from law enforcement as they work to keep everyone safe.
— Brad Little (@GovernorLittle) August 1, 2026

Hicks urged anyone with information about the shooting to reach out to law enforcement.
“Anyone with information related to this incident who has not already spoken with law enforcement is asked to contact dispatch at 208-735-4357,” a Twin Falls PD press release said.
Several videos posted to social media appear to show a man wearing a black shirt and jeans carrying a large rifle.
One depicts him shooting the front windshield of a parked Tesla, while another shows the man carrying the rifle and walking through the In-N-Out drive-thru.
Twin Falls Police said in a Facebook post that roads in the area, including the Perrine Bridge linking the city with Interstate 84, were closed but have since reopened.
St. Luke’s Health System issued a “critical alert” urging the public to avoid its Magic Valley hospital unless there’s an emergency.
Boise State Public Radio will update this story as more details become available.



Idaho officials responded in statements and social media posts about the shooting:
Idaho Gov. Brad Little, in an X post: “Idahoans, join me in keeping the Twin Falls community in your prayers as law enforcement and first responders respond to an active shooter situation near In-N-Out. Please avoid the area and follow directions from law enforcement as they work to keep everyone safe.”
Idaho Democratic Party chairwoman Lauren Necochea, in an emailed statement: “All of Idaho is grieving after the shooting in Twin Falls. Families are facing losses they never should have had to endure, and a community is struggling to understand how an ordinary day could end in such horror. My heart is with loved ones mourning innocent lives taken, the victims who were injured, and everyone whose sense of safety was shattered. Tragedies like this reveal the worst of what people can do, but also the best of who we can be. I am deeply grateful for the first responders and neighbors who moved toward danger, cared for others, and showed up when they were needed most. In the days ahead, may we carry that same compassion and courage forward and make sure the people of Twin Falls do not face this alone.”
Idaho Republican Party chairwoman Dorothy Moon, in an emailed statement:
“I am grateful that the threat to the community has ended and that there is no longer an ongoing danger to the public. Our hearts go out to the families who have lost loved ones, those who were injured, and everyone who is anxiously awaiting news about family and friends.
Idaho has always been a place where neighbors look out for one another and families can live in peace. Today’s tragedy is a heartbreaking reminder that senseless acts of violence can touch any community.
I want to express my deepest gratitude to the law enforcement officers, EMS personnel, and other first responders who responded with courage and professionalism under unimaginable circumstances.
I ask all Idahoans to join me in praying for the victims, their families, the people of Twin Falls, and everyone involved in the response and recovery. May God bring comfort to those who are grieving, healing to those who were injured, and strength to the entire community in the difficult days ahead.”
U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, in a social media post: “I’m monitoring the news out of Twin Falls of an active shooter situation. I urge locals and visitors to obey all directions from law enforcement, avoid the area, and report any suspicious activity immediately. I’m grateful for the swift response of Idaho’s first responders.”
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, in a social media post: “Vicki and I are monitoring the shooting in Twin Falls. We pray for the safety of all involved and thank the brave first responders on scene.”
U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho, in a social media post: “My team and I are closely monitoring the situation in Twin Falls.
I am disheartened to learn of the senseless loss of life. Please join me in praying for the victims’ families, the surrounding community, our brave law enforcement officers and first responders on scene, and all those affected by this tragedy.”
U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson, R-Idaho, in a social media post: “I am aware of the shooting in the area of In-N-Out in Twin Falls. My team is closely monitoring the situation as more information becomes available from the Twin Falls Police Department.
I am praying for everyone affected and for the brave first responders who are on the scene.”



Idaho Capital Sun editor Christina Lords contributed to this report.
