name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana nonresident tourism spending increased to $5.6 billion last year
description: A near-record number of out-of-state visitors spent roughly $5.6 billion while traveling to and through Montana in 2025, money powering one of the state’s strongest economic sectors through tourism-oriented businesses. That’s according to the latest report on annual nonresident visitation to Montana conducted by the University of Montana’s Institute for Tour[...]
text:
A packed parking lot at Logan Pass in Glacier National Park. (NPS/Jacob W. Frank)A near-record number of out-of-state visitors spent roughly $5.6 billion while traveling to and through Montana in 2025, money powering one of the state’s strongest economic sectors through tourism-oriented businesses.
That’s according to the latest report on annual nonresident visitation to Montana conducted by the University of Montana’s Institute for Tourism and Recreation Research, released last month. The quarterly nonresident research has been ongoing since 2009 and involves surveyors conducting more than 21,000 annual surveys at airports, rest areas and gas stations across the state. 
In 2025, roughly 13.2 million visitors — about 500,000 fewer than 2024, which was a record — spent around 12% more during their travels through the state compared to 2024, increasing the impact to the state’s economy to record levels. 
The $5.6 billion out-of-state travelers spent in Montana directly supported $4.1 billion in local economic activity through purchases of gasoline, groceries and retail, use of services such as lodging, outfitters and guides, and costs of license and entrance fees. 
An additional $3.1 billion of indirect impacts to economic activity — such as from purchases made by travel-related businesses and employees — drove a total of more than $7.1 billion into the state’s economy. 
Visitor spending directly supported an estimated 52,610 jobs, according to ITRR data, comprising roughly 1-in-11 Montana workers. 
That’s a significant jump from last year, when data estimated only around 38,240 Montanans worked directly in the tourism sector. 
The Institute estimates the tourism industry makes up around 18% of jobs in Montana — outpacing healthcare (15%), government (13%), agriculture (4%) and mining, oil and gas (1.2%). 
Visitors also generated more than $360 million in state and local taxes, which is estimated to have reduced the average tax burden on Montana households by $740, another increase from last year. 
The 4% decrease in visitation from 2024 still ranks as the second-highest visitation for the state on record. 
The visitation figures track with recent data released by the National Park Service showing that Yellowstone National Park saw the second highest number of visitors on record in 2025, while Glacier National Park notched its third busiest year. The two parks are listed as top attractions by visitors, serve as anchors for the state’s outdoor economy, and are crucial to local communities.  
Both parks are also near record visitation so far in 2026. 
Beyond visiting the state’s two national parks, public lands in general, and the state’s scenic beauty, is listed as an overall draw for tourists, with a majority of travelers using public lands to hike, sightsee and look for wildlife.
Results from the ITRR continue to track with data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis that show Montana’s outdoor recreation sector makes up 5% of the state’s economy, the third highest contribution of any state. 
Nonresident visitor spending, not adjusted for inflation. Graphic by ITRR
Here are some highlights from the 2025 visitor spending data. 
13,242,000
Estimated total nonresident visitors in 2025, the second highest ever.
$5.6 billion
Overall nonresident traveler spending in Montana during 2025.
$1,166,200,000
Amount tourists spent on gasoline and diesel statewide, the top expenditure category.
$1,119,180,000
Amount spent in bars and restaurants by out-of-state visitors last year
$191,560,000
Amount nonresidents spent specifically on “Made in Montana” products 
20%
Expenditures related to lodging, comprising hotels (12%), short term rentals (7%) and campgrounds and RV Parks (1%).
5.2 nights
Average length of stay in Montana. Tourists stay longest in the summer, an average of 6.21 nights.
46%
Percentage of tourists who visit the state from July-September. The fewest visitors, 11%, travel between January and March.
41%
Visitors who came to Montana solely for vacation. 23% of visitors were just passing through, 19% visited friends and family and 11% were here on business. One percent of visitors came just to shop.
6%
Visitors from Canada heading south of the border — a third fewer than in 2024 due to tariffs and inflation
33%
Estimated number of tourists who arrived from either Idaho, Washington or North Dakota
3,304,757
Estimated number of tourists who arrived via plane, a nearly 6% jump from 2024.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Hearing for Project Jupiter data center’s air quality permit application rescheduled to September
description: A public hearing over whether the New Mexico Environment Department should issue an air quality permit for the controversial Project Jupiter data center is being rescheduled to September, according to newly filed documents.
text:
Aerial photos taken on June 26, 2026, show the construction site for Project Jupiter, the Oracle and OpenAI data center project planned for southern New Mexico. (Courtesy of Alexa Reynaud, Food & Water Watch, with aerial support provided by LightHawk)A public hearing over whether the New Mexico Environment Department should issue an air quality permit for the controversial Project Jupiter data center is being rescheduled to September, according to newly filed documents.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The hearing officer presiding over the matter had previously scheduled the hearing to begin in October. At a scheduling meeting this week, attorneys representing Project Jupiter’s developers requested that the hearing begin earlier, arguing that the October hearing date would risk giving New Mexico Environment Department staff too little time to make a final decision on whether to issue the permit before their Nov. 23 deadline.
Max Shepherd, the hearing officer, told attorneys gathered at the scheduling hearing that he was not going to reschedule it. He said he would keep the October hearing date and examine his options to push out NMED’s Nov. 23 deadline.
However, two days later when NMED published his written scheduling order on its website, it showed he rescheduled the hearing by more than a month. It is now set to begin Sept. 14 and “continue as necessary” at the Sunland Park Multi-Generational Center.
“What happened between Monday morning, when he denied their motion for a new schedule, and Wednesday night?” Colin Cox, senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, which has intervened in the case, told Source NM. “It’s highly concerning.”
Cox on Friday filed a new motion requesting that Shepherd revert back to the previously scheduled October hearing date.
Maslyn Locke, senior attorney for the New Mexico Environmental Law Center, who has represented residents in lawsuits related to Project Jupiter, said the air quality permit case is among the most complex — and fast-moving — air quality complex cases she’s seen in her career. Under the revised scheduling order, she said attorneys will not have enough time to review the “thousands” of pages of the administrative record, catch their expert witnesses up to speed and prepare for oral arguments by the time the hearing begins in less than two months.
“Rushing this through is going to create more problems,” she said. “The department is neglecting the fact that once this thing is built, it’s really impossible to undo it.”
Shepherd, the hearing officer, when contacted by Source NM, said he could not comment on the rescheduling.
A spokesperson for the state Environment Department in a statement said the department “remains committed to meeting its statutory deadlines no matter the hearing date.”
At Monday’s scheduling meeting, Jennifer Bradfute, an attorney representing Project Jupiter developer Yucca Growth Infrastructure, argued that the hearing needs to happen as soon as possible.
Bradfute said her client would stand to lose $325 million per month, beginning in November.
“This project will start to abandon employment opportunities in New Mexico and there are many kids from the labor unions who want to be placed in jobs,” Bradfute said during the meeting. “We really do need this to go to hearing as soon as possible. The state is at jeopardy to lose the project entirely, and I’m not blowing smoke as I state that.”
At a Doña Ana County Board of Commissioners meeting earlier this week, Executive Vice President of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Mahesh Thiagarajan and STACK Infrastructure Chief Development Officer Bobby Hollis presented the project’s latest job numbers days before an annual report on the matter was due.
Hollis said at the meeting that the project employed nearly 700 New Mexicans during its ongoing construction. To date, it has employed nearly 2,800 construction workers and generated $734 million of contracts with New Mexico suppliers, according to their joint presentation.
The duo also told commissioners that they’re committing to 100% carbon-free energy matching by 2031.
County commissioners had previously set a Friday deadline for Project Jupiter’s developers to file an annual jobs report. However, that report was not readily available Friday afternoon.
In an email to Source NM, a Doña Ana County spokesperson said the report would contain personally identifying information for Project Jupiter employees and that county leaders “will be working with our legal team to get a form of the summary posted on the county’s website as soon as possible.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma appeals court tosses out stalking conviction related to man’s YouTube rant
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – A Bryan County man’s decision to post a 40-minute rant about his ex-wife on YouTube doesn’t constitute stalking, the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals ruled. In an order released Thursday, the state’s high court for criminal matters ordered the case against Lon Brandon Meeks, 45, dismissed. The high court ruled that the […]
text:
The Oklahoma Judicial Center is the headquarters of the Oklahoma Supreme Court and Court of Criminal Appeals. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – A Bryan County man’s decision to post a 40-minute rant about his ex-wife on YouTube doesn’t constitute stalking, the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals ruled.
In an order released Thursday, the state’s high court for criminal matters ordered the case against Lon Brandon Meeks, 45, dismissed.
The high court ruled that the state’s anti-stalking law is designed to “shield a person from unwanted conduct,” not “censor someone from randomly talking negatively about a third party to others.” The court said the law prohibits contact “directed toward” a person, not “communication about a person.”
Meeks, who was prosecuted in Bryan County District Court, was sentenced in 2025 to five years in prison, with the last two suspended. 
Meeks entered prison on July 15, 2025, and was released to supervision on May 11, according to the Oklahoma Department of Corrections.
A call to Meeks’ attorneys seeking comment was not returned Friday as of publication.
The Attorney General’s Office, which represented the state in the appeal, also did not immediately comment.
Meeks and his ex-wife separated in 2018 and divorced in 2019, and she obtained a protective order against him in 2019 that was extended to five years until April 2025, according to the appeal’s court decision.
The protective order barred him from contact, directly or indirectly, including calls, texts, emails, or communications on social media platforms even if not sent directly to her, according to the court.
The ex-wife’s boss sent her a May 2023 video by Meeks titled “One reason men shouldn’t get married,” according to the opinion. 
In it, Meeks says he is expressing his freedom of speech. 
In the profanity-laced video, which remained posted to YouTube on Friday, Meeks says negative things about the judicial system, his ex-wife, several other people and describes how he believes he was unfairly treated. He also graphically describes sex acts. 
“Meek’s post was undeniably about his ex-wife, and we are not indifferent to the embarrassment and harmful emotional toll being the subject of a spiteful rant concerning one’s personal life can have, especially in such a public forum as YouTube,” the opinion said. “It does not necessarily follow, however, that the offending post in this case was directed toward Meeks’ ex-wife, and this case illustrates that difference.”
The court wrote in its order that Meeks’ actions were “somewhat akin to the frustrated, drunken bar patron venting to everyone in the vicinity of his voice about the fallout from a bad romance and divorce.”
The court wrote that venting on social media platforms unfortunately often has a more widespread audience.

title: Losses mount for bills and lawmakers seeking to rehash pandemic disputes in South Dakota
description: Pandemic-era political disputes may be fading in South Dakota after lawmakers who proposed COVID-19-related bills during the 2026 legislative session failed to enact their proposals, and some of the legislators who sponsored or supported the bills either lost their primary races or aren’t seeking reelection. Six pieces of failed legislation would have shield[...]
text:
The South Dakota House of Representatives chamber on Feb. 3, 2026, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Pandemic-era political disputes may be fading in South Dakota after lawmakers who proposed COVID-19-related bills during the 2026 legislative session failed to enact their proposals, and some of the legislators who sponsored or supported the bills either lost their primary races or aren’t seeking reelection.
Six pieces of failed legislation would have shielded doctors and pharmacists from liability for providing prescription drugs unapproved by the Food and Drug Administration for COVID treatment, labeled blood donated by people who’ve received COVID vaccines so vaccine skeptics could avoid receiving it, banned employers and schools from requiring genetic-based immunizations such as some COVID vaccines, restricted the actions cities can take to fight a pandemic, and urged a lawsuit against China for its alleged role in causing the pandemic. 
Four of the bills advanced from the House Health and Human Services Committee to a vote of the full House, where they were rejected. The two others failed in other committees.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The members who voted in favor of all four of the bills that advanced out of the House Health and Human Services Committee were Republicans Dylan Jordan of Clear Lake, Josephine Garcia of Watertown, Bobbi Andera of Sioux Falls, Tony Kayser of Sioux Falls, Brandei Schaefbauer of Aberdeen, Logan Manhart of Aberdeen, and Heather Baxter of Rapid City.  
Jordan, Garcia, Andera, Kayser, Manhart and Baxter lost their primary races on June 2, which means they won’t be able to seek reelection in November. Baxter later secured the Republican nomination for secretary of state and is running for that post in November. Schaefbauer did not run for reelection.
Allie Alvine, founder of South Dakota Families for Vaccines, said the combination of legislative defeats and electoral losses could indicate that vaccine skepticism no longer carries the political strength it did during and immediately after the pandemic.
“But we’re not taking our foot off the gas,” Alvine said. 
Her organization intends to continue lobbying lawmakers about the benefits of vaccination, such as preventing serious illness that could lead to hospitalization or death, reducing the spread of infections, lowering health care costs and strain on medical systems, and completely or nearly eliminating diseases such as smallpox, polio, diphtheria and measles.
‘No known exposures’ after measles detected in Brookings county child, health department says

Schaefbauer said the bills she supported were meant to address an unresolved fight over who controls medical decision-making in South Dakota. She didn’t talk to hospital officials about the bills, she said, alleging they “made a lot of money off” the “COVID-scam-demic.”  
COVID-19 has been listed as a cause of 3,190 deaths in South Dakota, including about 2,900 over a two-year stretch from 2020 to 2022. 
Rep. Nick Fosness, R-Britton, serves on the House Health and Human Services Committee, works as a healthcare administrator and won his primary election. He opposed the four measures that came through the committee. 
“They seemed like hangover effects from COVID,” he said.
Fosness said that after a few weeks on the committee, it became clear that testimony from medical and healthcare groups would not stop the four bills.
“Regardless of the facts and logic presented from the field, those bills were going to pass the committee and head to the floor,” he said.
The composition of House committees is selected by the leaders of the majority Republican Party. After 16 incumbent Republican South Dakota lawmakers lost their seats in June’s primary, new leadership is expected for the legislative session that begins in January. 
In addition to the bills that passed the House Health and Human Services Committee, the House Judiciary Committee rejected Schaefbauer’s resolution urging a lawsuit against China. The Senate State Affairs Committee rejected a bill from Sen. Tom Pischke, R-Dell Rapids, that would have restricted the actions cities can take in response to a pandemic.
Pischke is facing two felony counts for allegedly filing documents to get candidates for county party positions on the June 2 primary ballot without those candidates’ knowledge. He has pleaded not guilty, and lawyers in the case have said a potential plea deal is being discussed. In response, Pischke dropped his reelection campaign, leaving the Republican Party to choose a replacement candidate to run against an independent in November.



This year’s failed COVID-related bills
COVID-19-related bills that failed in this year’s legislative session, and the electoral status of each bill’s sponsor: 
HB 1163 

Would have prohibited public and private employers from requiring “genetic-based vaccinations,” defined to include mRNA and similar technologies used to create the COVID-19 vaccine. The bill would have allowed the state attorney general to impose penalties of up to $10,000 for violations, with limited exemptions, including health care settings, lawfully required student vaccines, and the military. 
SPONSOR: Republican Rep. Bobbi Andera of Sioux Falls failed to win her June 2 primary election. 

HB 1171 

Would have required blood donation centers to ask donors whether they have ever received a COVID-19 or mRNA vaccine and to label the blood accordingly. 
SPONSOR: Republican Rep. Josephine Garcia of Watertown failed to win her June 2 primary election. 

HB 1210

Would have prohibited any employer, school, state agency, or local government from requiring COVID-19 vaccination as a condition of employment, enrollment, or access to services or benefits. 
SPONSOR: Republican Rep. Josephine Garcia of Watertown failed to win her June 2 primary election. 

HB 1068

Would have authorized pharmacists to dispense ivermectin or hydroxychloroquine — neither of which has been approved by the FDA for COVID treatment — and added liability protection for them. 
SPONSOR: Republican Rep. Bobbi Andera of Sioux Falls failed to win her June 2 primary election.

SB 145

Would have prohibited local governments from adopting health measures that affect activities in private residences or businesses, or from taking actions that could be interpreted as interfering with constitutional rights, including during a public health response.  
SPONSOR: Republican Sen. Tom Pischke of Dell Rapids withdrew his bid for election. 

HCR 6008

Would have urged the South Dakota attorney general to file a lawsuit against China and other entities, alleging responsibility for the COVID-19 pandemic and seeking $100 billion in damages.
SPONSOR: Republican Rep. Brandei Schaefbauer of Aberdeen did not seek reelection.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Two North Carolina US House races are now toss-ups, top forecaster says
description: North Carolina Democrats are closing the gap in two key congressional races in the state, political forecasters say, despite a new district map passed last year aimed at boxing them out of close House seats. Sabato’s Crystal Ball, one of the top-cited election forecasts in the U.S., updated its assessment of North Carolina’s 1st and […]
text:
The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., amid fog on Dec. 10, 2024. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)North Carolina Democrats are closing the gap in two key congressional races in the state, political forecasters say, despite a new district map passed last year aimed at boxing them out of close House seats.
Sabato’s Crystal Ball, one of the top-cited election forecasts in the U.S., updated its assessment of North Carolina’s 1st and 11th congressional districts from “Leans Republican” to “Toss-up.” They’re among 13 House seats in the country whose odds have moved toward Democratic candidates.
The rating changes follow similar Democratic momentum in the U.S. Senate race, where former Gov. Roy Cooper’s commanding lead in fundraising and the polls over Republican opponent Michael Whatley shifted the contest to “Leans Democratic.” And Democratic candidates in the state have seen unusually strong fundraising numbers powered by a surge in small-dollar donations.
NC Senate passes a new voting map to flip another seat in Congress to the GOP

Both seats, analyst Kyle Kondik wrote, would be difficult for Democrats to win in most election years, but President Donald Trump’s unpopularity has helped create strong headwinds for Republican candidates as voters have soured on the party in power.
For Rep. Don Davis, D-N.C., the 1st District incumbent, a win would put an ironic twist on North Carolina Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting effort, as the new map was explicitly aimed at drawing him out of office.
“Davis has already won a pair of tough races in different, albeit less red, versions of this seat in recent years,” Kondik wrote. “Davis will be facing a rematch with his 2024 opponent, Laurie Buckhout, and there is also a Libertarian in the race that Democrats hope will ease Davis’s path to victory.”
Meanwhile, Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., faces a difficult reelection bid in the 11th District because he faces a well-funded opponent with strong ties to the region. Edwards is also in the midst of a scandal over a House Ethics inquiry into an alleged affair, which he denies, and he has struggled to raise money for his reelection bid this year.
“Edwards’s challenger is Jamie Ager (D), who has fundraised well and whose grandfather held a version of this seat in the 1980s,” forecaster Kyle Kondik wrote. “The district backed Trump by a shade under 10 points, so it’s also clearly red-leaning, but, again, the environment could sand down some of that generic Republican lean, and Edwards has some problems.”
Cook Political Report, another top forecaster, also shifted their rating of the 11th District race toward Edwards, moving it from “Likely Republican” to “Leans Republican” last month. They did the same in Davis’s contest in December.
Ager campaign manager Grayson Barnette said in a statement that the movement in the race shows voters want a candidate who will be there for western North Carolina.
“Jamie is building a broad coalition across Western North Carolina because voters are ready for someone who is authentic — someone who will show up, deliver and put this district ahead of Washington politics,” Barnette said. “We’re glad the national handicappers are taking notice, but ratings don’t win elections, people do. We’re going to keep doing the work.”
The campaigns for Davis, Edwards, and Buckhout did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Key legal resource for immigrant kids to expire with federal contract, advocates say
text: WASHINGTON — Bryan Chavez knows that having access to legal representation as an unaccompanied minor can be a lifeline.In 2017, immigration officials separated him from his mother and brother at the southern border, as they were caught up in the family separation policy of the first Trump administration. The 15-year-old remained in a detention center for children, knowing that if he were sent back to Mexico, he would likely die at the hands of the cartel who threatened to kill him, his brother and father. “Everything changed when attorneys from (the Immigration Defenders Law Center) arrived,” he told reporters during a press conference Friday. “For the first time, someone explained what was happening. As a child, I couldn't understand why I was being separated from my mother.”Chavez, who is now a case worker at the same center that provided him legal services as an unaccompanied minor, worries about what will happen to the thousands of immigrant children who are set to lose their legal representation at midnight Saturday. That’s because the Trump administration declined to renew a federal contract with nonprofits that provide legal aid services to more than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children. Chavez, along with a handful of advocates and attorneys for immigrant children, detailed their concerns during a virtual press conference about the end of the contract. They warned that it will lead to children being quickly deported, because without a lawyer, fewer than 10% of immigrant children win the right to remain in the United States while their case goes through immigration court. “For many of them, an attorney can be the difference between fear and hope, separation and reunification, or even life and death,” Chavez said. “I came to this country asking for help. The children I work with today are asking for the same thing.”No reimbursements to lawyersFor more than six months, the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is part of the Department of Health and Human Services, has not reimbursed $65 million to the Acacia Center for Justice, which distributes the federal funding to roughly 100 organizations across the country who provide legal representation to unaccompanied children in immigration cases. The Acacia Center for Justice has said those funds are being withheld because attorneys refused to hand over to the Trump administration sensitive case data from the unaccompanied children, such as medical records and the types of legal relief the minors are seeking. “For months, Acacia has been negotiating in good faith with the government to find a way to continue representing unaccompanied children who would be left without their trusted lawyers, and at the whims of an administration that seems intent on finding new and crueler ways to target and deport them as quickly as possible,” said Bilal Askaryar, communications director at the Acacia Center for Justice.HHS did not respond to States Newsroom's request for comment. ‘A lot of uncertainty’The Acacia Center for Justice’s chief of staff, Bettina Rodriguez Schlegel, said that on Wednesday, government officials submitted a solicitation notice giving the Acacia Center for Justice time to transition legal services to another provider. Rodriguez Schlegel said she doesn't know for sure to whom the Trump administration will contract legal services, but the administration is eyeing a small Texas state commission that aids low-income people with criminal defense representation. “What will happen on Monday morning when kids go to court?” she asked. “There remains a lot of uncertainty and a great deal of concern.”Sensitive jobAdditionally, with the contract ending, children who have experienced trauma will have to recount painful experiences to attorneys who might not have the proper training. That can cause more anxiety, depression or post-traumatic stress for kids, said Dr. C. Nicholas Cuneo.Cuneo is an assistant professor of pediatrics and medicine at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and the executive director at HEAL Refugee Health and Asylum Collaborative, which provides trauma-informed healthcare services to immigrants.“A trusted attorney can buffer that harm, explaining an incomprehensible process, providing consistency and safety, protecting a child's interests, and connecting them to healthcare, school, housing, and other essential support,” he said. “Abruptly severing that relationship can not only reactivate the abandonment and powerlessness from which children are trying to recover, but really cause direct physical and mental health injury.”Cuneo said Congress recognized those consequences, and created the Unaccompanied Children Program to provide funding for legal representation of migrant children. Erin Maxwell, a social worker at Legal Services for Children in California, said so much of their training is in providing trauma-informed legal services.“I'm afraid that if a group of attorneys that were not trained on working with children, were not trained on providing trauma-informed legal services, that children wouldn't be able to fully participate in their cases (to share their stories),” she said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. lawmakers urged to preserve SNAP benefits, assist farming industry at committee hearing
description: Emily Scolnick is a 2026 Dow Jones News Fund intern at the Pennsylvania Capital-Star. Food bank executives and a union leader urged Democratic lawmakers to “protect SNAP at all costs” and help support Pennsylvania’s farming and agriculture industries amid rising costs at a committee hearing Friday. The state Senate Democratic Policy Committee meeting, led by[...]
text:
Chip-enabled cards for Pennsylvania's SNAP beneficiaries, like the Maryland version pictured above, could soon be a reality in the commonwealth. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Emily Scolnick is a 2026 Dow Jones News Fund intern at the Pennsylvania Capital-Star.
Food bank executives and a union leader urged Democratic lawmakers to “protect SNAP at all costs” and help support Pennsylvania’s farming and agriculture industries amid rising costs at a committee hearing Friday.
The state Senate Democratic Policy Committee meeting, led by Sen. Nick Miller (D-Lehigh) and Senate Minority Leader Jay Costa (D-Allegheny), focused on the need to lower grocery costs and the impact of federal policies on Pennsylvania’s food and farming industries. 
State Secretary of Agriculture Russell Redding said that even as the federal government’s values and priorities have changed, Pennsylvania’s commitment to affordability has not. 
“The strong farms and strong businesses and strong communities are not competing priorities. They’re inseparable,” he said. “Affordability doesn’t begin at the checkout lane. It begins with building food systems that are resilient, competitive, and work for everyone.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Allegheny County Executive Sarah Innamorato emphasized that as grocery prices have sharply risen since 2020, outpacing wage increases across the state, families are struggling to accept a “new normal.” 
“We’re not asking ourselves, ‘What do we want to buy?’ but rather, ‘What can we afford this week?’” she said. “We’re stretching every dollar, weighing price against nutrition, quantity against quality.” 
Pennsylvania has experienced some of the highest grocery price hikes in the country, according to data from Consumer Affairs. Wendell Young, the president of United Food & Commercial Workers Local 1776, said the uncertain state of the food and agriculture industry has made things increasingly difficult for employers, workers, and family-owned businesses. 
The entrance to a Big Lots store in Portland, Oregon. (Stock photo by hapabapa/Getty Images)
“The cost of the Trump administration makes it impossible for employers in this chaotic environment that this president’s caused,” he said. “The constant carousel of what is subject to tariffs and what isn’t, the lack of guidance from the Department of Homeland Security on what class of immigrant workers are allowed to stay in our country or not, and the modeling on how the Big Beautiful Bill will impact SNAP benefits for Pennsylvania consumers all contribute to this uncertainty.” 
Young said he believes the Trump administration’s tariffs have caused plant closures, stagnant wages, and hiring freezes. His union, which represents over 35,000 members, has lost over 6,000 jobs since Trump’s election. 
He added that a slaughterhouse in Montgomery County is slated to close on Aug. 14, eliminating another 1,400 jobs. 
The tariffs “make it more difficult to be able to run a plant in Pennsylvania where we don’t have a lot of cattle ranches nearby,” Young said. “So it’s an industry-wide problem right now, but it’s been exasperated by the tariffs and the immigration policies of this administration.” 
A western Pennsylvania farm. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
Sen. Judy Schwank (D-Berks), the minority chair of the Senate Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee, said the price of meat is a continuous issue for consumers. 
“It’s become almost unaffordable,” she said, urging support for local farmers. “We’re all looking for lower prices, but we have to remember that people need to make a living as well.” 
“In the wealthiest country in the world, we have people who can’t buy chicken,” added Sen. Nick Pisciottano (D-Allegheny). “This is a complete failure and a big, big problem that we need to address.” 
Redding said that international conflicts like the Russia-Ukraine war and the limited use of the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. and Israel launched attacks against Iran have caused issues with the fertilizer supply among the nation’s farmers. 
“We have placed in others’ hands, really, the basic ingredients in growing our crops,” he said. He urged the state to provide economic development assistance to further innovative efforts to increase the domestic fertilizer supply. 
Leaders of several food banks in the Pittsburgh area told lawmakers they are seeing an increasing number of people turning to their organizations for assistance.
“More than 1.7 million Pennsylvanians don’t have enough food to meet their nourishment needs. More than half a million children are food insecure,” said Julie Bancroft, the CEO of Feeding Pennsylvania. “Almost 20% of Pennsylvania’s children don’t have enough food to eat, and that obviously impacts their ability to learn and to grow.” 
Bancroft added that 10% of older adults in Pennsylvania experience food insecurity, while nearly half of the food insecure live above the SNAP eligibility threshold — earning too much to qualify for benefits, but not enough to adequately provide for their families. 

One year after ‘One Big Beautiful Bill Act’: 98K fewer Pennsylvanians on SNAP


Over 98,000 Pennsylvanians have lost access to SNAP benefits since President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law last year, according to estimates from the state Department of Human Services. 
“Grocery prices have increased 33% between 2019 and 2026 … that’s the largest jump in 50 years,” Bancroft said, citing data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. “They’re all being priced out of the grocery stores and being forced to make impossible choices about rent, medicine, utilities, transportation, and food.” 
Colleen Young, the Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank’s director of government affairs, said her organization distributed 830,000 more pounds of food in the 2026 fiscal year as it did the year prior. She added that their on-site food pantry in Duquesne is averaging 200 visitors per day. 
“Government assistance is ensuring that agencies without a food budget can source more food and keep up with rising demand,” she said. 
Bancroft said their biggest need is for lawmakers to “protect SNAP at all costs.” 
“If we don’t have the support of SNAP and our state food programs, we can’t, we simply can’t meet the need that will result from folks not having access to SNAP benefits,” she said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Fate of Medicare, Medicaid emerge as key issue in 2nd District race
description: On the 61st anniversary of President Lyndon B. Johnson signing Medicaid and Medicare into law, the fate of the healthcare programs are emerging as a key issue for the candidates looking to replace Congressman Jared Golden.  Republican nominee Paul LePage has said he will protect Social Security and Medicare, but has a history of opposing […]
text:
A dozen members of the Maine People’s Alliance gathered at Cascade Park — just down the street from Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center — to commemorate the 61st anniversary of Medicaid and Medicare on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)On the 61st anniversary of President Lyndon B. Johnson signing Medicaid and Medicare into law, the fate of the healthcare programs are emerging as a key issue for the candidates looking to replace Congressman Jared Golden. 
Republican nominee Paul LePage has said he will protect Social Security and Medicare, but has a history of opposing Medicaid expansions while he was governor. In contrast, Democratic nominee Matt Dunlap is campaigning on support for Medicare-for-all.
“There are some places where economic gain and greed just do not belong, and that is the care of our neighbors,” Dunlap said at a press conference in Bangor Thursday. “People should not have to live in fear of a slip and fall on the ice driving them into bankruptcy.”
Dunlap said healthcare is the issue he has heard about the most on the campaign trail. He said it’s important to celebrate the anniversary, but also focus on the future of Medicare and Medicaid, federal programs that elderly, low income and people with disabilities rely on. President Donald Trump’s administration has made large cuts to Medicaid in particular, leaving millions without healthcare. 
“Where we go next is going to be a long effort to bring national healthcare — Medicare for all, universal healthcare, whatever you want to call it — so that people can finally get that burden off their shoulders of how they take care of themselves and their families,” he said. “So that they can use their energy and their drive and their abilities to make their lives better for themselves and their families, instead of constantly living in fear that they’re going to go bankrupt because they just got a diagnosis.” 
Matt Dunlap, the Democratic nominee for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, held a press conference in Bangor Thursday to commemorate the 61st anniversary of Medicaid and Medicare. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)
Dunlap criticized LePage for his record on healthcare while serving two terms as governor. While in office, LePage oversaw dramatic cuts to the state’s healthcare programs, significantly reducing coverage for low-come adults. 
He vetoed five bills that would have expanded MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program. And after voters in 2017 approved a referendum to expand MaineCare with 59% support, LePage refused to implement it. 
At the time, LePage said he was not obligated to expand the program until it was funded, but he vetoed a bill that would have funded the expansion. Several groups challenged LePage’s refusal in court, but the legal battles dragged the issue out until the end of his term. 
The expansion only began Democratic Gov. Janet Mills took office in 2019, using her first executive order to implement it.
Dunlap also criticized LePage’s support for many of President Donald Trump’s healthcare policies passed in the massive 2025 government funding package. These included new Medicaid work requirements and other changes to eligibility impacting disabled and elderly people, unhoused people and some immigrants. 
Maine legislators tried to make up for some of those cuts this session, but failed to pass a sweeping $250 million bill that would have reinstated some lost federal healthcare benefits at the state level.
“He mentioned that the Big Beautiful Bill was the greatest thing in the world for people in Maine, and I just don’t see it,” Dunlap said. “I don’t see how taking things away, resources away from our working families, does anything but drive them further into doubt and uncertainty.” 
Brent Littlefield, spokesperson for LePage’s campaign, said in a statement that Dunlap, the former Maine secretary of state and current state auditor, has “failed to show he understands healthcare or government funding.” 
He said, if elected, LePage will prioritize keeping hospitals open, and medical practitioners in Maine. 
“Paul LePage has gone on record repeatedly with concerns that government-run healthcare programs will not properly reimburse healthcare facilities for their real costs and the chickens have come home to roost with hospital service impacts,” Littlefield said.
Last year, the advocacy group Protect Our Care estimated that 330 hospitals nationwide — including two in northern Maine — were at risk of immediately shutting down due to reductions in Medicaid funding included in congressional Republicans’ tax law. 
Last year, national nonprofit Third Way estimated that Medicaid cuts would cost Maine hospitals more than $66 million per year in revenue, and $24 billion nationwide.
Former Republican Gov. Paul LePage was endorsed by President Donald Trump in his bid to represent Maine’s 2nd Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives. (Photo via LePage campaign)
Littlefield also cited LePage’s record as governor, particularly when the state government paid off $750 million in debt to hospitals.
LePage’s 2011 supplemental budget included $70 million in state funds to pay the hospitals, which was matched by federal money resulting in $248 million in payments to dozens of hospitals.
He also signed a 2013 bill to pay off an additional $183.5 million debt to Maine hospitals, which drew an additional $307 million in federal matching funds. But Democrats at the time criticized LePage for stalling the payments, after he vetoed an earlier bill that would have made the payments and expanded Medicaid. 
LePage blamed the hospital debt on the state’s 2002 Medicaid expansion under former independent Gov. Angus King, who now serves as the state’s junior U.S. senator, which was funded by a cigarette tax increase. 
“Paul LePage literally saved hospital services, and healthcare, for Mainers,” Littlefield said. “Matt Dunlap has done nothing.”
Allegations of fraud
State and national Republicans have targeted Medicaid programs in Maine and elsewhere as having what they describe as extensive “waste, fraud and abuse.” 
Both the state and federal government are investigating claims of improper payments made to some providers. 
On a May visit to Bangor, Vice President JD Vance said the Trump administration will be cracking down on Medicaid fraud in the state. Vance urged the crowd to vote for LePage and other Republicans, while criticizing Democrats as difficult to work with.
Addressing the crowd before Vance’s arrival, LePage said, “JD Vance being here today is a warning shot to every fraudster, scam artist and corrupt bureaucrat protecting our broken system.” 
In the most recent federal review, Maine’s Medicaid payment error rate was 2.4%, which is lower than the national average of 3.2%. And only about 0.1% of total program spending was confirmed by federal reviewers to be definitively incorrect. 
Dunlap said Thursday that the claims of fraud are really meant as broad attacks on Medicaid. 
“They’re not interested in rooting out fraud,” Dunlap said. “They’re interested in getting rid of Medicaid. So let’s not be fooled by the rhetoric that’s coming out of the administration.”
What others are saying 
During Thursday’s press event, Dunlap supporters spoke about the importance of expanding Medicare and Medicaid, and said that Dunlap is the right candidate for the job.
“We can do better,” said Erin Oberson, a nurse with the Maine State Nurses Association, which represents 4,000 nurses and caregivers. “We can guarantee high-quality healthcare to everyone in this country. As we celebrate Medicare’s birthday, let’s remember that this fight is not over. Let’s take with us the spirit of the activists that won in 1965 and carry that into our fight today.” 
Dr. Noah Nesin said in his 40-year career, he has seen how important Medicare and Medicaid is to help people afford healthcare. And he knows how devastating the recent federal cuts will be.
“The cuts coming out of Washington from the Big Beautiful Bill will strip coverage from tens of thousands of Mainers, push our rural hospitals even closer to the brink and stretch nurses, doctors and caregivers even thinner than we already are,” he said. 
But Republican leadership has argued that LePage is the best option to tackle healthcare for Maine.
National Republican Campaign Committee spokesperson Maureen O’Toole said no one is stronger on healthcare. 
“He kept hospitals open, ensured Mainers had access to care and did it all without raising taxes a single cent,” she said in a statement. “Meanwhile, out of touch Democrat Matt Dunlap wants to completely decimate Maine’s health care system by implementing socialist policies like government-run healthcare that undermine access to care.” 
Maine Republican Party senior advisor Jason Savage echoed the sentiment.
“Democrats complaining about the current state of Maine’s healthcare after single-party control needn’t point fingers at Paul LePage, who left the system stabilized — all they have to do is look in the nearest mirror,” Savage said in a statement. 
VP Vance rails against Democrats, immigrants at anti-fraud rally in Bangor

Just a few hours after Dunlap’s press conference, a dozen members of the Maine People’s Alliance gathered at Cascade Park — just down the street from Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center — to commemorate the anniversary. 
They held signs, and as passing cars honked in support, chanted, “Protect our healthcare, no more warfare.”
Gabriel Veilleux, a field canvasser for the progressive political action group, said that a fifth of Maine residents in the 2nd Congressional District have MaineCare and the Trump administration’s cuts to Medicare and Medicaid are unacceptable.
“A lot of people can’t even afford insurance, and without it, they’re terrified of getting sick,” Veilleux said. “A lot of people on MaineCare are losing their coverage, and a lot more will lose coverage if the budget cuts keep unfolding the way they are. This is not the way that things should be, and Paul LePage in Congress would just make it 10 times worse for us.”
Thomas Poling, a field manager for the Maine People’s Alliance Bangor canvass team, said he speaks with people every day who are terrified of losing their coverage, or already can’t afford their insurance. And that LePage has already hurt Mainers when he was governor. 
“We think that in his time as governor, he did a lot of damage to Maine’s social safety net and to social programs that lots and lots of people all over the state rely on,” Poling said. “And we think that to have him in Congress in Jared Golden’s former seat would be damaging not just for Maine, for the whole country.”
Eesha Pendharkar contributed to this reporting.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware Paid Leave distributes $7.6 million during first six months
description: More than 1,700 medical, parental and family-care claims were paid as the state launched one of its largest new employee-benefit programs in decades WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware’s new paid family and medical leave program distributed more than $7.6 million in benefits during its first six months, according to figures released by the Delaware Department of Lab[...]
text:
More than 1,700 medical, parental and family-care claims were paid as the state launched one of its largest new employee-benefit programs in decades
WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware’s new paid family and medical leave program distributed more than $7.6 million in benefits during its first six months, according to figures released by the Delaware Department of Labor.
First six months bring 1,760 paid claims
The Division of Paid Leave paid 1,760 claims between Jan. 1 and June 30, the department said. The program issued more than 11,000 individual payments, including payments to employees using intermittent leave rather than taking one continuous period away from work.
Medical leave represented 45.5% of approved claims, followed closely by parental leave at 43%. Family caregiver leave accounted for 11.5%, while qualifying military-related leave represented 0.1%.
“We’re thrilled to see initial results like this, validating the importance of Delaware Paid Leave in our state,” Delaware Paid Leave Director Chris Counihan said in a statement. “People are utilizing the program as they need to, whether it’s for a medical emergency or something that has been planned.”
Counihan encouraged workers who may qualify to file claims and determine whether they are eligible.
Benefits replace part of workers’ wages
Based on the state’s reported totals, the program paid an average of about $4,300 per approved claim during its first six months. Because some employees receive multiple payments or take intermittent leave, that figure does not represent an average weekly benefit.
Eligible employees can receive up to 80% of their average weekly wages, with benefits capped at $900 per week. Employees may receive up to 12 weeks of paid leave during a 12-month period, depending on the type of qualifying leave and the limits established under the law.
The program covers qualifying absences involving an employee’s serious health condition, the care of a family member with a serious health condition, bonding with a new child or certain needs arising from a family member’s overseas military deployment.
Supporters point to financial safety net
Supporters describe the program as a financial safety net for working Delawareans who might otherwise have to choose between earning a paycheck and caring for themselves or a family member. The Department of Labor pointed to national savings data showing that many families have limited reserves to cover an extended loss of income.
Skeptics question long-term costs
Program skeptics, however, are asking whether the current payroll contribution rate will be sufficient to support benefits over the long term. The first six months of claims demonstrate demand for paid leave, but the state’s announcement did not show whether payroll collections are keeping pace with benefit payments, administrative expenses and future obligations. Critics worry that higher-than-expected use could eventually require increased contributions from workers and employers.
Small-business owners have expressed concerns about the cost and complexity of complying with the law, particularly when an employee takes extended or intermittent leave. Even when wage-replacement benefits are paid through the program, employers may face scheduling disruptions, overtime costs, temporary hiring expenses and additional administrative work. Skeptics also argue that the state should release more detailed financial and performance information before describing the early results as proof of long-term success.
Program funded through payroll contributions
The program is financed through payroll contributions that began in January 2025. Employers may require employees to pay a portion of the cost through payroll deductions. Employers may also use an approved private plan instead of participating directly in the state-administered program.
The Healthy Delaware Families Act was sponsored by Sarah McBride while she served in the Delaware Senate. McBride, now Delaware’s member of the U.S. House, described the legislation as a way for employees to address major family and medical needs without losing their entire income.
The law was signed in May 2022, and benefits became available Jan. 1, 2026. It marked one of the largest expansions of Delaware’s employee-benefit system in decades.
Financial questions remain unanswered
For employers and policymakers, the early claim figures provide the first significant measure of how the program is being used. However, the Department of Labor’s announcement did not include the total amount collected through payroll contributions, the program’s current fund balance, administrative costs, the number of claims denied or the number of applications still pending.
Those figures will be important in determining whether the program is operating efficiently and whether its financing remains stable without requiring higher payroll contributions in future years.
TO GO BOX   Delaware Paid Leave

What it provides: Partial wage replacement for qualifying medical, parental, family caregiver and military-related leave.
Maximum benefit: Up to 80% of an employee’s average weekly wage, capped at $900 per week.
Maximum leave: Up to 12 total weeks during a 12-month period, depending on the qualifying reason.
Who may qualify: Eligible employees who work primarily in Delaware and meet employment and hours-worked requirements.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RI attorney general candidates find common ground before policy clashes emerge late in debate
description: Rhode Island’s four Democratic candidates seeking to succeed term-limited Attorney General Peter Neronha found common ground on most issues during a two-hour debate Thursday evening, though the cordial tone turned more contentious toward the end. Kim Ahern, Keith Hoffmann, Rep. Jason Knight, and Rep. Joe Solomon sat before over 100 people inside the communit[...]
text:
Democratic candidates for Rhode Island attorney general participate in a debate hosted by OpenDoors at the Southside Cultural Center in Providence on July 30, 2026. From left: Keith Hoffmann, Jason Knight, Kim Ahern, and Joe Solomon. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island’s four Democratic candidates seeking to succeed term-limited Attorney General Peter Neronha found common ground on most issues during a two-hour debate Thursday evening, though the cordial tone turned more contentious toward the end.
Kim Ahern, Keith Hoffmann, Rep. Jason Knight, and Rep. Joe Solomon sat before over 100 people inside the community room at Southside Cultural Center in Providence for a “justice and policy debate” hosted by OpenDoors. The discussion was moderated by Nick Horton, co-executive director of the nonprofit that helps formerly incarcerated people, those struggling with addiction and other unhoused people. 
Questions from Horton and other community advocates focused on police accountability, bail reform and automating the expungement of criminal records — issues candidates each supported to varying degrees.
On police accountability, Knight and Hoffmann both backed creating a process to revoke the certification of officers found to have committed serious misconduct. Solomon said the attorney general should enforce the law “against any individual who commits any offense,” while Ahern pledged to reopen field offices in overpoliced communities so residents could more easily share their experiences with prosecutors.
“Those closest to the problem are closest to the solution,” Ahern, a former state prosecutor and previous chairperson of the Rhode Island Cannabis Control Commission, said.
All four candidates rejected blanket policies to hold probation violators without bail and instead endorsed individualized assessments. 
Differences began to show when a community advocate asked whether the four supported closing the Donald W. Wyatt Detention Facility in Central Falls amid its close partnership with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Knight was generally supportive, but said he wanted to meet with community members first since the facility also houses federal pretrial detainees whose families would otherwise have to travel out of state.
“Generally speaking, I think Wyatt was a mistake,” Knight said.
The other three candidates also stressed the potential consequences of moving detainees farther from Rhode Island.
“A lot of them will end up in Florida, Texas, and New Hampshire,” Hoffmann, who was previously chief of policy and senior in Neronha’s office, said. “Our attorneys will not as easily be able to bring habeas petitions on their behalf.”
They became more critical of each other when asked how they would distinguish themselves on policy. 
Knight, who has spent the last 10 years representing parts of Barrington and Warren in the State House, highlighted his support for the 2019 law that codified Roe v. Wade at the state level.
“Joe Solomon voted against that bill,” he said. “That’s a lukewarm response to an issue from one of the candidates up here on an issue that is critical to all of us.”
Keith Hoffmann, a Democrat running for Rhode Island Attorney General, takes notes during a debate on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Solomon, who has represented portions of Warwick since 2015, defended his vote by noting it came before the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization. The 2022 ruling overturned the constitutional right to an abortion and gave states the authority to ban the procedure.
“Once that Dobbs decision happened, it changed the entire landscape,” Solomon said. “I am committed to protecting a woman’s right to choose.”
The moderate Democrat further noted his votes in favor of the 2023 law allowing state Medicaid money and state employee health insurance to fund abortion care, and legislation passed in 2024 that defends doctors’ ability to provide reproductive health services and gender-affirming care.
Hoffmann also noted Solomon’s vote last year against the law that bans the manufacture and sale of certain assault-style weapons, which took effect at the start of July.
“I guess everyone is going to come after me tonight,” Solomon said.
Solomon agreed that illegal weapons should be taken off the streets, but that state gun laws may target lawful gun owners
“Even though they have fancy names and whatnot, if you look at the details they encompass people just like you and me who may potentially be committing a crime because of how it was written,” he said.
The final question — how each candidate would approach lawsuits against President Donald Trump’s administration — quickly shifted back to police accountability, re-entry programs and the diversity of the attorney general’s office after several audience members raised the issues.
Hoffman responded with the need for the state to further fund the Police Officers Commission on Standards and Training. Knight pledged to work with State House leaders to get more resources for housing and other resources to help formerly incarcerated people get back on their feet. Ahern said she would hire more diverse attorneys with lived experiences if she were elected. Solomon closed the debate pledging to stick around and answer everyone’s questions — as did the other candidates who held small conversations with community members.
Early voting begins Aug. 20 for the Sept. 9 primary. The winner will face Republican Alan Gordon in the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota paid leave payroll tax rate to remain the same next year
description: Minnesota’s paid leave payroll tax will remain at 0.88% in 2027, shared between workers and their employers, the state announced Friday — but a new actuarial analysis indicates the program may need to increase the rate in 2028 to abide by state law. The state Department of Employment and Economic Development said in a press […]
text:
Minnesota Capitol. Photo courtesy of Minnesota House Public Information Services.Minnesota’s paid leave payroll tax will remain at 0.88% in 2027, shared between workers and their employers, the state announced Friday — but a new actuarial analysis indicates the program may need to increase the rate in 2028 to abide by state law.
The state Department of Employment and Economic Development said in a press release that the actuarial analysis conducted by Spring Consulting Group shows the program will remain sustainable in 2027 with the current 0.88% payroll tax rate, or 88 cents for every $100 in earnings, split equally between workers and bosses.
The announcement no doubt comes as a relief to Democrats running for reelection this year, after the program passed without a single Republican vote in the 2023 Legislature.
But DEED may be merely postponing the inevitable: State law requires that the program’s projected budget reserve at the end of each year doesn’t fall below 25% of paid leave’s total program expenditures, and the new analysis shows that it will do so in 2028.
The Spring Consulting Group projected that by 2028, Minnesota paid leave will bring in a revenue of nearly $1.3 billion but incur over $1.5 billion in expenses. The 2028 year-end balance is expected to be $200 million — about 13% of the program’s expenses. If the projections are correct, DEED will need to increase the payroll tax rate.
The report also shows that the total expenses this year — $1.3 billion — will outpace total revenue of $1.2 billion.
Paid leave grants Minnesota workers up to 12 weeks of family leave and 12 weeks of medical leave per year, capped at 20 weeks in a single year.
The analysis also did calculations assuming the state increases the payroll tax rate to 0.93%, but they show that the fund’s balance at the end of 2028 would still be expected to fall below 25% of expenditures.
DEED can’t increase the payroll tax rate above 1.1% unless the Legislature changes the law.
DEED Deputy Commissioner Evan Rowe in a statement to the Reformer said the analysis largely relied on data from other states’ programs when estimating Minnesota’s payment projections.
“That experience is useful, but Minnesota’s experience will undoubtedly be different, just as every state is different. We don’t want to overcorrect in 2027 for future-year scenarios which may not come to pass,” Rowe said.
More Minnesota-specific data collection, he said, “will allow for more detailed (and Minnesota-specific) actuarial projections into 2028 and beyond.”
Minnesota’ s paid leave program has become a commonly cited political issue in the midterm election cycle. Democrats are touting the popular benefit and its glitch-free rollout as a reason to elect them, while Republicans criticize the program for adding to Minnesotans’ tax burden.
Over 75,000 Minnesotans have claimed paid leave in 2026 so far, DEED said, totaling more than $600 million in partial wage replacement payments.
“The first six months of paid leave show Minnesotans are excited about the program and will continue using and depending on it to support themselves and their families,” DEED Commissioner Matt Varilek said in a statement.
Nearly every employer and worker in Minnesota qualifies for the paid leave program. It offers partial wage replacement for people who have welcomed a child into their home, are recovering from an injury or surgery or taking care of a loved one. Wages are determined by a wage-based formula, capped at $1,423 per week.
The program received an early spike in applications after its launch on Jan. 1, but the number has since tapered off. DEED has rejected over 40% of the total 126,000 applications it’s received, most commonly due to the lack of proper certification from healthcare providers and other documentation.
Minnesota lawmakers required DEED to conduct an actuarial analysis each year to determine the program’s solvency and required the agency to finalize the following year’s tax rate by the end of July.

title: Dept. of Corrections offering up to $6,000 in hiring and retention bonuses to recruit new officers
description: A month after Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed legislation that would have provided tens of millions of dollars to the Florida Department of Corrections (FDC) for pay increases for correctional officers, the department announced on Friday that it is now offering up to $6,000 in hiring and retention bonuses at select prisons throughout the state. They […]
text:
Columbia Correctional Institution in Lake City is one of the Florida prisons where correctional officers could be eligible for $5,000 retention bonuses. (Photo from Florida Dept. of Corrections website)A month after Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed legislation that would have provided tens of millions of dollars to the Florida Department of Corrections (FDC) for pay increases for correctional officers, the department announced on Friday that it is now offering up to $6,000 in hiring and retention bonuses at select prisons throughout the state.
They include a new $1,000 hiring bonus at 13 correctional institutions and, at “select institutions,” an already existing $5,000 retention bonus for eligible officers, providing up to $6,000 in total incentives.
“The Florida Department of Corrections is committed to investing in the men and women who choose to serve and support Florida’s public safety mission,” said Corrections Assistant Deputy Secretary of Institutions Hope Gartman in a written statement.
Correctional officers in Florida prisons make $22 an hour. In January, then-Secretary Ricky Dixon asked a legislative committee for $374 million to raise base pay for corrections officers, probation officers, inspectors, and non-uniformed staff that would raise their pay to $28 an hour.
Dixon told the Senate Appropriations Committee on Criminal and Civil Justice that it would have been “the most significant pay increase I’ve seen in three decades in this business,” adding that it would “make a major impact” in retaining corrections officers, who often leave for other law enforcement agencies that pay more. (Dixon recently stepped down from the department.)
The Legislature ultimately authorized a $91.5 million pay increase for Department of Corrections employees, which would have boosted the minimum correctional officer base pay to $24 an hour.
However, that funding was wiped out when Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed legislation last month that included $50 million a year in corrections capital projects for 40 years and mandated construction of a new 600-bed corrections hospital in Gilchrist County funded by bonds.
In his veto letter, DeSantis said he had offered the $374 million in funding that Dixon had requested, but “it was not contingent on incurring massive new debt obligations for constructing a new prison hospital.”
He went on to describe the funding proposal a “D.C. swamp approach to correctional pay” that he called “a game I am not willing to pay.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont is not for sale
description:
Our housing crisis isn't about scarcity. It's about who owns the homes we already have.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont is not for sale.
text:
This commentary is by John Bossange, president, and Jerry Ward, a board member, of Better (not bigger) Vermont.
The pro-development advocates finally got it right. Vermont is in trouble but not for the reasons offered in a recent VTDigger opinion piece written by representatives of the Vermont Futures Project, the Vermont Professionals of Color Network, the Vermont Business Roundtable, the Vermont Chamber of Commerce, Let’s Build Homes and the Lake Champlain Chamber.
Vermont is in trouble because there is a giant “For sale” sign posted at our borders, and our economic policies encourage investors and speculators to purchase available lots and recently built homes.
Vermont is in trouble because no matter what the profit-making industries tell us, a housing shortage, if it even exists, is not the root cause of our problems.
Vermont is in trouble because we’re letting anticipated population growth and speculative housing need guide our development policy.
Vermont is in trouble because development advocates rarely account for the long-term upkeep and carrying costs of infrastructure and essential municipal services.
Vermont is in trouble because building more homes does not yield enough revenue to offset tax increases to cover those costs.
Vermont is in trouble because companies like BETA Technologies and OnLogic may struggle to pay future employees enough to move here and afford a mortgage on a new home.
Vermont is in trouble because the development industry too often overlooks the environmental impacts of building on open fields, clear-cutting natural forests and disturbing wetlands.
The development advocates got it right when they wrote “the data is clear,” but then used a deeply flawed analysis to promote their pro-growth, profit-making agenda with their own self-serving data and avoided the facts that Vermonters care about the most.  

READ MORE

Vermonters cannot afford a mortgage on a $750,000 home. That’s a real fact. Our nonprofit organization, Better (not bigger) Vermont, has documented the cost of a new-build home in various communities in Chittenden County, and that’s the average price.  
We are pricing out our next generation because the industry that could make a big difference chooses to build to the open market and not to the working Vermonter’s pocketbook. Why don’t we hear more about that?
Vermonters care deeply about the negative environmental impacts on our clean air, water, soil, the warming planet and our climate crisis. That should be clear data presented by the development advocates as well. Why has this not been a part of their messaging?
Today there are over 65,000 unoccupied homes in Vermont (19.4%), the second-highest percentage in the nation, many of them owned by investors, second-home owners and out-of-state, part-time residents. We would argue there is no real housing shortage in Vermont.  It is more accurately a wealth distribution problem. That’s an analysis you never read about in the promotional articles written by the development industries. Why not?
Vermonters are rightfully concerned about their property taxes. Building more homes directly increases our taxes because of the short- and long-term costs to build and maintain infrastructure and provide essential municipal services, such as police, fire and schools, which are never fully covered by impact fees or the growth in the grand list. Why is this never mentioned?
The authors of the recent commentary are correct when they state that the “data is clear” about our aging population, just as it is in many other parts of the United States. So, let’s be careful not to view this as a problem we can easily solve. It’s much bigger than Vermont.
Finally, the question is not simply about abundance or scarcity as the pro-development advocates suggest. We should plan to grow carefully, building up from scarcity and not down from anticipated abundance. Yes, we need more cottage industries that fit into the character of our state. But we must never use speculative population growth and theoretical housing needs to build homes. That is a dangerous precedent, and not appropriate for government intervention.
It’s time to slow down and take advantage of this opportunity to first do what is best for Vermont and its citizens. Our rural character, our natural environment, our cities, towns and villages all deserve to be cared for before the financial interests of the development lobbyists and profiteers who try to overwhelm us with more fear, myths and panic. 
Vermont may be in trouble, but not for the reasons argued by the pro-development forces. Our uniquely beautiful state with its abundant natural resources and beauty, and our great citizenry, should never be on the market. We are not for sale.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont is not for sale.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming will pay Star Plunge owner $1.8M to settle hot springs dispute
description:
Under tentative agreement, state will reimburse longtime concessionaire Luehne for capital and business interests. It awaits the attorney general’s approval. 
The post Wyoming will pay Star Plunge owner $1.8M to settle hot springs dispute appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming State Parks has reached an agreement with Star Plunge owner Roland Luehne that signals an end to two years of litigation and the long-term closure of the popular Thermopolis aquatic facility. 
The tentative settlement still needs final approval from the Wyoming attorney general’s office. If approved, it will conclude all litigation and stipulate that the state reimburse Luehne’s company $1.8 million, which is the appraised value of the concessionaire’s capital investment and ongoing concern in the Hot Springs State Park business minus the value of the state-owned land. 
The agreement would effectively end a saga that began with the state’s 2024 decision to select a new operator for the Star Plunge, which the Luehne family had managed for 50 years. That decision sparked controversy. On one side, proponents argued that a new operator could spruce up the park’s aging facilities and breathe fresh life into the hot springs destination. Opponents said it would Disney-fy the park, price patrons out and leave a local family in the lurch. 
“I’s been a long road, and we’re looking forward to the next steps,” Deputy Director for Wyoming State Parks Nick Neylon said. “It’s exciting.”
The agreement would also result in reopening the Star Plunge, which closed in January 2025 after Luehne’s short-term management agreement with the state expired. The timeline details aren’t yet concrete as the state needs to ensure facility safety, Neylon said, but he hopes it can reopen within months. 
The spring-fed mineral waters of Star Plunge and Hot Springs State Park have been a destination for residents and visitors for centuries. Native Americans visited the waters, which they prized for their healing qualities, long before white settlers. The original 1-square-mile park land was established through a treaty. 
A boy swims in the Star Plunge in May 2024. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 
The land was later ceded to the state on the stipulation that there always be free public access to the therapeutic waters. What began as a reserve became the state park in 1929. With its midcentury drive-in motif and water slides, the Star Plunge has been a favorite of families since at least 1950.
Lawsuit and closure
Hot Springs State Park, which sits on the banks of the Bighorn River, features playgrounds, a boardwalk over mineral terraces, multi-use trails and aquatic facilities. 
As landlord, Wyoming holds concessionaire agreements with park operators. That includes the Star Plunge and Teepee aquatic facilities and two hotels. All four were built decades ago and are in various stages of aging. Wyoming also operates a state bathhouse, which is free and open to the public per the treaty language.
The dispute between Wyoming State Parks and Luehne is most simply understood as a landlord-tenant disagreement.
The Luehne family had operated the Star Plunge since 1975, when Wolfgang and Christine Luehne bought it and took over a 50-year concessionaire lease. Their son, Roland, bought it from them in 2012.
Guided by a vision for an updated park laid out in a 2016 master plan, Wyoming State Parks in 2024 selected Wyoming Hot Springs LLC as the next leaseé through its request-for-proposal process. Wyoming Hot Springs LLC’s primary representative, Mark Begich, a former U.S. senator from Alaska, also purchased in late 2023 the Tepee Pools. Hot Springs LLC’s application laid out plans for significant upgrades and renovations. 

Star Plunge owner Roland Luehne stands in front of historic signs decorating a wall at the aquatic facility. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 

The state’s selection promised to effectively evict the Luehne family from Star Plunge. Luehne had been operating on a string of short-term management agreements since 2008.
Luehne contested the process in a pair of lawsuits filed by his company, C&W Enterprises. They accused Wyoming State Parks of exceeding its authority and violating regulations. Luehne argued the state was attempting to dislodge him without fairly compensating him for the improvements. 
The state, meanwhile, defended its process in court filings and statements. The court dismissed Luehne’s first lawsuit, and the second one, over compensation, was set for an October trial. 
Budget note
The Wyoming Legislature’s 2026 budget earmarked $3 million for “concessionaire remedies” at Hot Springs State Park. Lawmakers amended the language to mandate that the state undertake a full appraisal of the capital investment and ongoing concern of the business. 
That legislation is what allowed the state to offer Luehne the reimbursement in the settlement, Neylon said. 
State Parks has long been anxious to reopen the facility, according to representatives, and this will allow the new concessionaire a clear path to make significant investments in the facilities. 
“We are excited to partner on the long-term enhancement and modernization of these facilities, to ensure a safe, exceptional, and affordable experience for Wyoming residents and visitors,” Dave Glenn, director of the Wyoming Department of State Parks and Cultural Resources, said in a press release.
